chapters.summary: Council staff welcome attendees to the Committee on Immigration hearing, ask that electronic devices be silenced, and explain testimony slips and front-desk rules. The Chair is then invited to begin.
chapters.title: Staff opens hearing and gives housekeeping instructions

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: Good morning and welcome to today's New York City Council hearing for the Committee on Immigration.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: Ladies and gentlemen, at this time, we please ask that you silence all electronic devices.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: If you would like to fill out a testimony slip, then please see one of the sergeant arm officers.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: Moving forward, no one is to approach the front desk.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: Chair, you may begin.

chapters.summary: Chair Elsie Encarnación calls the hearing to order and identifies herself as Chair of the Committee on Immigration. She announces the oversight topic and the four items: Intro 739, Proposed Intro 1077-A, Proposed Intro 1078-A, and Resolution 729.
chapters.title: Chair Encarnación calls hearing to order and introduces agenda

utterances.speaker: Elsie Encarnación
utterances.text: I am calling this hearing to order.

utterances.speaker: Elsie Encarnación
utterances.text: Good morning, everyone.

utterances.speaker: Elsie Encarnación
utterances.text: I am Councilmember Elsie Encarnacion, Deputy Whip of the New York City Council and Chair of the Committee on Immigration.

utterances.speaker: Elsie Encarnación
utterances.text: Thank you for joining us.

utterances.speaker: Elsie Encarnación
utterances.text: Today, we will be examining the current state of immigration enforcement activity in New York City and hearing four bills.

utterances.speaker: Elsie Encarnación
utterances.text: Introduction 739, Proposed Introduction 1077A, Proposed Introduction 1078A, and Resolution 729.

chapters.summary: Chair Encarnación thanks administration representatives, the public, and council colleagues who joined, including Councilmembers Hanks, Brewer, Avilés, and Public Advocate Jumaane Williams. She acknowledges their presence before beginning her substantive remarks.
chapters.title: Chair thanks attendees and introduces colleagues and public advocate

utterances.speaker: Elsie Encarnación
utterances.text: I'd like to thank

utterances.speaker: Elsie Encarnación
utterances.text: all of the representatives from the administration, members of the public, and my council colleagues who have joined us here today, including Councilmember Hanks, Councilmember Brewer, Councilmember Aviles, and

utterances.speaker: Elsie Encarnación
utterances.text: I'm going to throw you in there, Javani, and our public advocate, Javani Williams.

chapters.summary: Chair Encarnación describes two years of mass deportation, family separation, and ICE raids in neighborhoods from Washington Heights to Corona. She recounts the Marble Hill shooting of Oscar Belgal, a 28-year-old Dominican New Yorker, while his 5-year-old son was in the car.
chapters.title: Chair describes federal immigration enforcement and Marble Hill shooting

utterances.speaker: Elsie Encarnación
utterances.text: For nearly two years, our country has reckoned with a presidential term that has sown chaos, instilled fear, and enacted a program of mass

utterances.speaker: Elsie Encarnación
utterances.text: deportations, apologies, and family separation in immigrant communities.

utterances.speaker: Elsie Encarnación
utterances.text: In recent months, those realities have played out in an excruciating way.

utterances.speaker: Elsie Encarnación
utterances.text: In our own neighborhoods from Washington Heights to Sunset Park to Corona, where ICE has abducted community members during street raids.

utterances.speaker: Elsie Encarnación
utterances.text: This came to head last month on a bustling residential street in Marble Hill, where ICE agents shot Oscar Belgal, a 28-year-old New Yorker from the Dominican Republic, while he was in his car with his 5-year-old son.

utterances.speaker: Elsie Encarnación
utterances.text: Mercifully, the child was not physically harmed.

utterances.speaker: Elsie Encarnación
utterances.text: But Bogal has since been transferred to the notorious Metropolitan Detention Center.

utterances.speaker: Elsie Encarnación
utterances.text: Bogal's attorneys allege that the left side of his face remains numb following the shooting, that he struggles to hear anything out of his left ear, and that the bullet remains lodged in his body.

chapters.summary: Chair Encarnación says New York City has always been a city of immigrants and praises residents organizing to protect immigrant neighbors. She explains the hearing will examine immigration enforcement activity and whether the city's response upholds protective laws and funds legal services.
chapters.title: Chair frames NYC as city of immigrants and purpose of oversight hearing

utterances.speaker: Elsie Encarnación
utterances.text: New York City has been and will always be a city of immigrants.

utterances.speaker: Elsie Encarnación
utterances.text: Now more than ever, ordinary New Yorkers in all five boroughs are coming together to protect our immigrant neighbors.

utterances.speaker: Elsie Encarnación
utterances.text: They have affirmed their values and positive vision for a city that safeguards and empowers immigrants to thrive alongside all New Yorkers.

utterances.speaker: Elsie Encarnación
utterances.text: For centuries, this city has been a beacon for families across the globe who have sought freedom from persecution, a better future for their children, and the ability to earn a living with dignity.

utterances.speaker: Elsie Encarnación
utterances.text: With today's oversight hearing, the Committee on Immigration will examine the current state of immigration enforcement activity in New York City and assess whether the city's response to it lives up to the promise of our city and the bravery of New Yorkers.

utterances.speaker: Elsie Encarnación
utterances.text: We will explore the mayoral administration's efforts to uphold our protective laws, fund legal services and know your rights trainings, refrain from facilitating civil immigration enforcement actions, and empower the working people of this city.

utterances.speaker: Elsie Encarnación
utterances.text: This council remains ready to work with the administration to stand up against oppressive immigration policies and to protect our community's futures.

chapters.summary: Chair Encarnación introduces Proposed Intro 1077-A, which would prohibit NYPD from detaining individuals beyond their release time without a judicial warrant. She explains it would allow NYPD to honor civil immigration detainers only with a judicial warrant for a non-immigration law enforcement purpose and would remove the 48-hour exception.
chapters.title: Chair introduces Intro 1077A on NYPD civil immigration detainers

utterances.speaker: Elsie Encarnación
utterances.text: Lastly, the Committee of Immigration will hear several bills, including two that I sponsor.

utterances.speaker: Elsie Encarnación
utterances.text: First, proposed introduction 1077A would prohibit the New York City Police Department from detaining an individual beyond the time when such person would otherwise be released from custody without a judicial warrant.

utterances.speaker: Elsie Encarnación
utterances.text: Proposed introduction 1077.

utterances.speaker: Elsie Encarnación
utterances.text: and A would allow the NYPD to honor civil immigration detainers by holding a person beyond their release date or notifying federal authorities

utterances.speaker: Elsie Encarnación
utterances.text: of a person's release only if federal immigration authorities present the NYPD with a judicial warrant and

utterances.speaker: Elsie Encarnación
utterances.text: such warrant is for a law enforcement purpose not related to immigration enforcement.

utterances.speaker: Elsie Encarnación
utterances.text: The bill would also examine an existing exception allowing the NYPD to honor a civil immigration detainer by holding a person for up to 48 hours beyond their release date under certain circumstances.

utterances.speaker: Elsie Encarnación
utterances.text: The removal of this existing exception would bring local law in line with New York case law, holding that such an action constitute a new arrest and seizure under both New York law and the Fourth Amendment of the U.S.

utterances.speaker: Elsie Encarnación
utterances.text: Constitution.

chapters.summary: Chair Encarnación introduces Proposed Intro 1078-A, which would similarly prohibit the Department of Correction from holding individuals beyond release without a judicial warrant. She says the bill would replace the conviction-based approach with a due process-based model.
chapters.title: Chair introduces Intro 1078A on DOC detainers

utterances.speaker: Elsie Encarnación
utterances.text: Second, proposed in Troll 1078 would similarly prohibit the Department of Corrections from detaining an individual beyond the time when such person would be otherwise released from custody without a judicial warrant.

utterances.speaker: Elsie Encarnación
utterances.text: The bill would allow DOC to honor civil immigration detainers by holding a person beyond their release date or notifying federal authorities of a person's release

utterances.speaker: Elsie Encarnación
utterances.text: only if federal immigration authorities present DOC with a judicial warrant and such warrant is for law enforcement purpose, not related to immigration enforcement.

utterances.speaker: Elsie Encarnación
utterances.text: If passed, these bills would

utterances.speaker: Elsie Encarnación
utterances.text: would replace the existing evidence, sorry, existing conviction-based approach

utterances.speaker: Elsie Encarnación
utterances.text: with a due process-based model by implementing an unequivocal judicial criminal warrant exception and streamlining our detainer laws.

utterances.speaker: Elsie Encarnación
utterances.text: I look forward to hearing the administration position on these bills.

chapters.summary: Chair Encarnación introduces Intro 739, sponsored by Councilmember Shahana Hanif, requiring agencies to train employees, contractors, and subcontractors on city resources law. The bill would also require publication of implementation protocols for DOC, Probation, and NYPD regarding detainer laws.
chapters.title: Chair introduces Intro 739 on agency training and implementation plans

utterances.speaker: Elsie Encarnación
utterances.text: Next, the committee will consider Introduction 739, sponsored by Councilmember Shahana Hanif,

utterances.speaker: Elsie Encarnación
utterances.text: in relation to requiring agency training and the publication of implementation plans concerning immigration enforcement and cooperation with non-local law enforcement agencies.

utterances.speaker: Elsie Encarnación
utterances.text: This bill will require agencies to train their employees, contractors, and subcontractors on the requirements of our city resources.

utterances.speaker: Elsie Encarnación
utterances.text: Law and to publish protocols for implementing and complying with that law.

utterances.speaker: Elsie Encarnación
utterances.text: The bill would apply the same training and protocol publication requirements to DOC, the Department of Probation, and the NYPD regarding the city's detainer laws.

utterances.speaker: Elsie Encarnación
utterances.text: I want to thank Councilmember Haney for introducing these bills.

chapters.summary: Chair Encarnación introduces Resolution 729, sponsored by Public Advocate Jumaane Williams, calling on New York State to pass the BUILD Act. She explains the BUILD Act would provide workforce development and capacity-building grants to expand legal representation for people facing deportation.
chapters.title: Chair introduces Resolution 729 and BUILD Act

utterances.speaker: Elsie Encarnación
utterances.text: Finally, the committee will hear Resolution 729, sponsored by Public Advocate Jumaane Williams, calling on New York State legislator to pass

utterances.speaker: Elsie Encarnación
utterances.text: and the governor to sign A2689-S4538 in relation to enacting the Building Up Immigration Legal Defense, or BUILD Act.

utterances.speaker: Elsie Encarnación
utterances.text: The BUILD Act would provide competitive workforce development and capacity building grants.

utterances.speaker: Elsie Encarnación
utterances.text: to eligible entities that are seeking to expand access to representation for individuals facing deportation by increasing the workforce and strengthening the legal service infrastructure needed to provide such representation.

utterances.speaker: Elsie Encarnación
utterances.text: No New Yorker should have to face the deportation dragnet without an advocate by their side.

utterances.speaker: Elsie Encarnación
utterances.text: And so I want to thank the public advocate for introducing it.

chapters.summary: Chair Encarnación thanks committee staff, including Senior Legislative Counsel Nicole Cata, Rebecca Barrilla, Navi Baines, and Florentine Cabor. She also thanks her chief of staff Stephanie Herrera and the Sergeant at Arms for making the hearing run smoothly.
chapters.title: Chair thanks committee staff and personal staff

utterances.speaker: Elsie Encarnación
utterances.text: And I would also like to thank my committee staff for the work on this hearing, including Senior Legislative Counsel Nicole Cata, Senior Legislative Policy

utterances.speaker: Elsie Encarnación
utterances.text: Analyst Rebecca Barrilla, Principal Financial Analyst Navi Baines, and Assistant Finance Director Florentine Cabor.

utterances.speaker: Elsie Encarnación
utterances.text: Finally, I would like to thank my staff, especially my chief of staff, Stephanie Herrera, and everybody working in the background to make this hearing run smoothly, especially our amazing Sergeant at Arms.

utterances.speaker: Elsie Encarnación
utterances.text: Did anyone else come in?

utterances.speaker: Elsie Encarnación
utterances.text: No?

utterances.speaker: Elsie Encarnación
utterances.text: Okay, I will now turn it over to the public advocate, Giovanni Williams, for brief remarks on his resolution.

chapters.summary: Public Advocate Jumaane Williams thanks Chair Encarnación and the Immigration Committee for holding the hearing. He introduces himself and notes his resolution on the BUILD Act.
chapters.title: Public Advocate Williams thanks committee and introduces remarks

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Chair.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: Good afternoon, everyone.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: As I mentioned, my name is Jermaine Williams.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: I'm a public advocate of the city of New York and the Knicks on a winning streak.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: I'd like to thank the chair in consternation.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: I always say the name wrong.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: I'm working on it.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: I apologize.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: And members of the Immigration Committee for holding this hearing and for the opportunity to share the statement.

chapters.summary: Williams says immigrants are students, coworkers, neighbors, and business owners who are fundamental to New York City. He describes aggressive federal enforcement that has destabilized communities, separated families, and left residents in constant fear.
chapters.title: Williams describes immigrant contributions and federal enforcement fear

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: New York City has forever and always been a home to immigrant communities from every single part of the world.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: Immigrants are students, co-workers, neighbors, business owners, and a fundamental part of the socioeconomic.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: and cultural fabric of New York City.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: At the same time, these same immigrant New Yorkers are dealing with the consequences of aggressive federal immigration enforcement that has destabilized communities, broken apart families, and left residents in constant fear.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: ICE has indiscriminately carried out arrests in workplaces, immigration court hearings, and routine check-ins, and infiltrated spaces where people seek assistance and support from the city.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: This summer in Flatbush, I was speaking to a roughly 80-year-old woman who now walks around with her passport.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: She's afraid of being stopped.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: The impact of these actions is not simply theoretical.

chapters.summary: Williams discusses Executive Order 13, which directed city agencies to examine ICE activity and report on its effects. He cites a May 2026 audit showing a 71% increase in ICE enforcement actions and rising federal presence in shelters and detainer requests.
chapters.title: Williams discusses EO 13 audit and ICE enforcement increase

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: In response to growing concerns about federal immigration enforcement activity in New York City, Executive Order 13 directed city agencies to examine and report on ICE activity and its effects on city services and facilities to...

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: To audit their internal policies and protocols on immigrant immigration enforcement, coordination, and report back to the mayor.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: According to the May 2026 audit that was produced, there was a 71% increase in ICE enforcement actions across New York City area between January 2025 and March 10, 2026, and an overall rising

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: federal presence inside city shelters, unauthorized entry incidents, and surging detainer requests.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: The audit also documented arrests at routine ICE check-ins.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: These incidents highlighted how individuals attempting to comply with immigration requirements are instead finding themselves separated from their loved ones and placed in detention.

chapters.summary: Williams describes transfers away from support networks, lack of medical care, unsafe detention conditions, and families losing income. He says fear of cooperation with federal authorities makes it harder for the city to provide services and maintain stability.
chapters.title: Williams describes detention conditions and community impacts

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: The repercussions of immigration detention extend far beyond the initial incarceration.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: Individuals are often transferred to facilities and away from their support networks, making it difficult for them to contact their legal representatives.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: I echo concerns about the reported lack of medical care and unsafe detention conditions.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: Reports that chronic illness left untreated, prescriptions are interrupted, physician coverage is sporadic or non-existent, and facilities are overcrowded and unsanitary.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: Families and communities of those essentially kidnapped face sudden loss of incomes and are understandably reluctant to reach out or receive government resources in fear of cooperation with federal authorities.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: This makes it more difficult for our city to reliably provide services and maintain stability.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: Today's oversight hearing is a crucial opportunity to examine the current state of immigration enforcement activity in New York City and how agencies are implementing laws to protect our immigrant residents.

chapters.summary: Williams says he supports all legislation heard today and speaks in depth about Resolution 729, which calls on Albany to pass the BUILD Act. He explains the bill would fund workforce development and capacity building to expand deportation defense.
chapters.title: Williams supports legislation and explains Reso 729 BUILD Act

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: I support all of the legislation heard today and want to speak in depth about my legislation, Reso 729, which calls on New York State legislature to pass and the governor to sign

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: Assembly Bill 2689, Senate Bill 4538, regarding enacting the Building Up Immigrant Legal Defense or BUILD Act.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: This legislation, sponsored by Senator John Liu and Assemblymember Catalina Cruz, who's here, would establish dedicated funding to provide workforce development and capacity building grants to scale up

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: the legal workforce and strengthen infrastructure to ensure more undocumented individuals have access to deportation events.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: In this way, the BUILD Act would support organizations, increasing their capacity to serve individuals and families navigating immigration court.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: This investment is particularly important as legal services

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: Legal service providers face an unprecedented increase in demand for the services.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: For immigrant New Yorkers, particularly those who protected status has recently been eliminated, children who have lost legal representation after federal funding cuts, and families navigating the needlessly difficult court system, these services are life-altering.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: Studies by the American Immigrant Council covering...

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: Fiscal years 2019 and 2024 found that only 26.9% of representative respondents were ordered removed, compared with 61.8% of unrepresented respondents.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: Expanding access to legal representation requires more than simply assisting people in navigating complex paperwork.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: We have to ensure that people grappling with the possibility of separation from their families and their homes understand their rights and have an advocate.

chapters.summary: Williams thanks the city for allocating $4.5 million to expand MOIA's immigration legal support hotline to seven days a week. He says the investment is a meaningful start but callers still face long hold times and need systemic change.
chapters.title: Williams discusses legal hotline funding and need for systemic change

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: I'd like to thank the city's recent allocation of $4.5 million to expand the Mayor's Office of Immigrant Affairs Immigration Legal Support Hotline to seven days a week.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: This investment will help ensure immigrant New Yorkers have greater access to free, confidential legal assistance and trusted information.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: It's a meaningful start.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: Of course, we need true systemic change.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: It must also be made to truly make this investment fruitful.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: Immigrant New Yorkers seeking assistance have reported lengthy hold times and instances in which they are promised a callback and often comes too late.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: Expanding the hotline's hours must be accommodated by improvements to ensure that callers can actually reach the correct resources and receive their timely assistance they need.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: It is absolutely critical that New Yorkers and New York City as a city funded them.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: by immigrants, as well as I always want to shout out the indigenous people and long-term black Americans who have been here for a long time.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: It maintains clear protocols and ensures that residents can trust their government with due diligence, keeping them safe.

chapters.summary: Williams describes how xenophobia kept families from coming forward after a building collapse in the 45th District. He also says ICE is training at Floyd Bennett Field and that ICE serves no purpose except making everyone less safe.
chapters.title: Williams cites building collapse and xenophobia; Floyd Bennett Field

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: I do want to also just point out the building collapse that recently happened in the 45th District, Councilman Farrell Lewis.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: What people may not know is because of the xenophobia, because of the anti-immigrant fears that people had, literally there were families who watched the building collapse who were afraid to come forward.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: They were afraid to speak about who may have been in the building.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: They were afraid to ask for assistance for themselves because of the xenophobia that's in here.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: People don't realize the intersecting problems that occur.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: Even when there's a tragedy, you're afraid to step forward.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: These policies make everyone unsafe.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: I now understand that ICE is practicing and doing work in Floyd Bennett Field.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: We do not want them here in New York, anywhere close in New York.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: They serve no purpose except to make everyone less safe.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: So thank you, Madam Chair, for having this hearing and for giving an opportunity.

utterances.speaker: Elsie Encarnación
utterances.text: Thank you, Public Advocate Williams.

utterances.speaker: Elsie Encarnación
utterances.text: I'd also like to acknowledge that we've been joined by Councilmember Joseph.

utterances.speaker: Elsie Encarnación
utterances.text: And I will now turn it over to an invited panel of witnesses.

utterances.speaker: Elsie Encarnación
utterances.text: Thank you so much for being here.

utterances.speaker: Elsie Encarnación
utterances.text: Assemblymember Catalina Cruz, can you please come up to the dais?

utterances.speaker: Elsie Encarnación
utterances.text: Jocelyn Atahulapa from Queens Neighborhood.

utterances.speaker: Elsie Encarnación
utterances.text: And please, excuse me for...

utterances.speaker: Elsie Encarnación
utterances.text: my pronunciation, and Naima Dehar from Arab American Family Support Center.

utterances.speaker: Elsie Encarnación
utterances.text: This will be our pre-panel, and you can begin when all are seated.

chapters.summary: Assemblymember Catalina Cruz introduces herself as representing District 39, including Corona, Jackson Heights, Elmhurst, Middle Village, and Rego Park. She thanks the committee for allowing her to testify on the reality facing immigrant and mixed-status neighbors.
chapters.title: Assemblymember Catalina Cruz introduces herself and district

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Catalina Cruz
utterances.text: Good morning, everyone.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Catalina Cruz
utterances.text: My name is Catalina Cruz, and I am the assembly member representing District 39 and serving Corona, Jackson Heights, Elmhurst, parts of Middle Village, and Regal Park in Queens.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Catalina Cruz
utterances.text: First, I'd like to thank Chair Encarnacion and the Immigration Committee for allowing me to testify on the reality that my immigrant and mixed-status neighbors are facing daily since President Trump took office and embarked on a coordinated attack on our communities.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Catalina Cruz
utterances.text: I first took office in 2019, and it has been my mission since then to represent and support the needs of all constituents, regardless of immigration status.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Catalina Cruz
utterances.text: But the reality of the last two years has forced me to reshift focus to provide additional support through legislation, funding, and the everyday work of my office to tackle the repercussions of a purposely broken immigration system.

chapters.summary: Cruz says since early 2025 her office has responded to ICE sightings and kidnappings by canvassing, providing know-your-rights information, and supporting families. She says ICE presence has grown from a couple of kidnappings a week to several every day.
chapters.title: Cruz describes office response to ICE kidnappings

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Catalina Cruz
utterances.text: Since late January, early February 2025, my office has been responding to eye sightings and kidnappings by preparing our neighbors and supporting them in the aftermath.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Catalina Cruz
utterances.text: We have

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Catalina Cruz
utterances.text: been doing this through canvassing of our neighbors, small businesses and community spaces in advance of any activity to educate them and provide them know your rights, the actual cards and any other information.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Catalina Cruz
utterances.text: During the kidnapping incidents, we respond in person as part of a network of volunteers to help warn the community and support neighbors as they are being kidnapped.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Catalina Cruz
utterances.text: In the aftermath, we work with the impacted families to secure legal representation and mental health services.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Catalina Cruz
utterances.text: This work has become increasingly difficult with the steady growth of ICE presence on our streets.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Catalina Cruz
utterances.text: We went from a couple of ICE kidnappings a week in 2025, more often than not without a warrant, to now seeing several ICE kidnappings every single day.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Catalina Cruz
utterances.text: The statistics gathered by many of the groups doing the work on the ground are clear, and that ICE is not really going after people with a criminal record, contrary to what the Trump administration would like us to believe.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Catalina Cruz
utterances.text: We have even seen ICE agents literally stand on a corner right next to a school and start pointing at people and picking them up as they walk by, simply because they look like immigrants.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Catalina Cruz
utterances.text: I want to walk us through the observations from our work and what we as a city and state elected officials, as well as agencies, can and should be doing.

chapters.summary: Cruz calls on NYPD to amend internal policies, provide training, and impose consequences for violations. She recounts an incident where ICE agents parked at a precinct and entered as if they worked there, and another where NYPD appeared to guard ICE during a kidnapping.
chapters.title: Cruz calls for NYPD policy changes and recounts precinct incident

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Catalina Cruz
utterances.text: First, the NYPD must amend its internal policies in relation to responding to incidents that involve ICE.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Catalina Cruz
utterances.text: This can mean additional training, clarification of existing policies, implementation of actual consequences for violations of said policies.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Catalina Cruz
utterances.text: On September,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Catalina Cruz
utterances.text: 2026, my team witnessed ICE agents driving to a local precinct and park in their parking lot and enter the precinct as if they work there.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Catalina Cruz
utterances.text: Later, when I raised the alarm, I was informed that according to the ICE agent, he went in seeking help because he was being chased by a mob.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Catalina Cruz
utterances.text: This so-called mob was actually two volunteers.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Catalina Cruz
utterances.text: One of them happened to be one of my staffers.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Catalina Cruz
utterances.text: Documenting the ICE agents activity in our community, something they have the right to do, and not chasing or threatening anyone.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Catalina Cruz
utterances.text: There was no actual cooperation from our understanding, but the perception to the community is that there was.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Catalina Cruz
utterances.text: And earlier in that month, earlier in the summer, we also saw a video in Jackson Heights that during a kidnapping of a neighbor,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Catalina Cruz
utterances.text: by ICE agents, the NYPD showed up, and it was almost as if they were facilitating or actually guarding the ICE agents during that activity.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Catalina Cruz
utterances.text: Again, if there was no cooperation, that is not the image that the community is getting.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Catalina Cruz
utterances.text: The law is clear in New York City.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Catalina Cruz
utterances.text: The NYPD does not cooperate or facilitate the work of ICE.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Catalina Cruz
utterances.text: Yet these interactions feel and look like facilitation, and they are going to erode any trust that the community still has on our local officers.

chapters.summary: Cruz calls on the Department of Education to train all personnel on rights and ICE encounters. She describes a father detained by ICE near three schools during morning arrival, with terrified families and students witnessing the detention.
chapters.title: Cruz calls for DOE training and recounts school-area detention

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Catalina Cruz
utterances.text: Second, the New York City Department of Education must provide training for all personnel, teachers, building staff, principals, everyone that's involved with our children, so that they understand not only their own rights when they encounter ICE,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Catalina Cruz
utterances.text: but what to do if it's with the children in school vicinity.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Catalina Cruz
utterances.text: On October 27, 2026, at approximately 7.30 in the morning, a father was detained by ICE after stepping out to move his vehicle for alternate side parking.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Catalina Cruz
utterances.text: The encounter escalated when he saw shelter in a nearby supermarket where four ICE agents forcibly dragged him out, barefoot and handcuffed him as he cried out for his daughter.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Catalina Cruz
utterances.text: The incident occurred during morning school arrival within a two-block radius of three schools, including one of our international high schools.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Catalina Cruz
utterances.text: My team witnessed terrified families running for safety, parents falling to the ground with their children, and students crying aboard a school bus as they watched the detention unfold.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Catalina Cruz
utterances.text: And at least nine ICE vehicles were reportedly present.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Catalina Cruz
utterances.text: Unfortunately, many school staffers were unprepared to respond because they had not received the necessary training to support families during ICE enforcement operations.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Catalina Cruz
utterances.text: Some schools opened their doors, as they've been instructed to do, to provide shelter while my team and community rapid response teams monitored and cleared the surrounding area to ensure that family and students could safely enter their schools.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Catalina Cruz
utterances.text: Even after my team and I made contact with a relative of the detained parent, we had to return to the streets because ICE vehicles remained idling in the community.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Catalina Cruz
utterances.text: The emotional impact was devastating, with nearby schools referring students that witnessed this incident to social workers to receive counseling following the traumatic experience.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Catalina Cruz
utterances.text: However, this trauma extends beyond students to their parents and their families.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Catalina Cruz
utterances.text: entire school system who also have to access mental health support.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Catalina Cruz
utterances.text: For many immigrant households, this has become an everyday reality, forcing parents to have to make heartbreaking decisions and have conversations with their children that they might not return home.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Catalina Cruz
utterances.text: No child should have to witness this and no parent should be forcibly detained away from their family, especially during

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Catalina Cruz
utterances.text: when they're trying to drop their kids off at school.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Catalina Cruz
utterances.text: When I arrived on the scene, it became abundantly clear from my conversations with the principals and educators and other members of the system that they did not know the basics of what to do

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Catalina Cruz
utterances.text: during the ICE operation and what they could and should do in response in order to protect these children.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Catalina Cruz
utterances.text: I do want to highlight that since then, in the aftermath, I've had great conversations with the superintendent of the district, the principals in our local school, and the chancellor and his team have been very open to hearing my suggestion and beginning to implement them.

chapters.summary: Cruz says the city and state must increase funding for legal services and rapid response. She describes racing to file habeas petitions and gather information after a neighbor is detained, and notes nonprofits lack capacity for emergency petitions.
chapters.title: Cruz urges legal services funding and rapid response capacity

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Catalina Cruz
utterances.text: Third, our city and state must increase funding to legal services and response mechanisms to protect our neighbors.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Catalina Cruz
utterances.text: After our neighbor has been kidnapped, we have just a few hours to submit a habeas and try to get an attorney for them before their transfer or worse, deported.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Catalina Cruz
utterances.text: We're racing against time to gather critical information like their personal details to locate them, their A number, any medical conditions, and whether they have minor children.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Catalina Cruz
utterances.text: Unfortunately, many nonprofit legal organizations simply don't have the capacity to take on emergency habeas petitions, which makes the process even more challenging.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Catalina Cruz
utterances.text: We also have to gather and submit all of this information to the Rapid Response Legal Committee.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Catalina Cruz
utterances.text: collaborative team in order to provide them potential legal action.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Catalina Cruz
utterances.text: Meanwhile, families are left waiting, terrified, and uncertain about their loved ones.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Catalina Cruz
utterances.text: Every minute matters.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Catalina Cruz
utterances.text: There are simply also not enough lawyers in this field.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Catalina Cruz
utterances.text: That is why in Albany I championed the legal services funding, and this year we got $82.48 million.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Catalina Cruz
utterances.text: I do want to thank our public advocate for introducing Resolution 1078, which would go hand in hand with this money to ensure not only that we're providing the services, but that we are training the attorneys, social workers, and everybody in the system to be able to do so.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Catalina Cruz
utterances.text: Additionally, while we have very dedicated volunteers, and I want to thank them infinitely because these people are going out every single day for free to support our communities as part of the response networks, it is simply not sufficient.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Catalina Cruz
utterances.text: The city and state at the very least must fund organizations to provide additional know your rights and rapid response canvas in order to better prepare our communities.

chapters.summary: Cruz highlights Albany legislation including A694 on immigration consequences of pleas, the Stunts Act on shock devices, and the Empire State Licensing Act. She thanks the committee and offers to answer questions.
chapters.title: Cruz highlights Albany bills and concludes

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Catalina Cruz
utterances.text: As I end, I would also like to highlight a few important pieces of legislation that I will be working with in Albany and I would love the support of the committee on within the coming future.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Catalina Cruz
utterances.text: A694 will require non-citizen defendants to be notified of potential immigration consequences before entering a plea to a misdemeanor or violation.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Catalina Cruz
utterances.text: A11692, or the Stunts Act, would prohibit shock gloves and other electrical shock devices from being sold or used in the state of New York.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Catalina Cruz
utterances.text: And A675, the Empire State Licensing Act, would ensure that New Yorkers can access professional, occupational, and commercial licenses.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Catalina Cruz
utterances.text: essences regardless of their immigration status.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Catalina Cruz
utterances.text: I want to thank you all again and I'm happy to answer any questions that you may have.

chapters.summary: Jocelyn Atahualpa introduces herself as a member of Queens Neighborhoods United since 2014. She says Corona, Jackson Heights, and Elmhurst are overrun with ICE and describes her daily routine checking for ICE activity and abductions.
chapters.title: Jocelyn Atahualpa introduces Queens Neighborhoods United

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jocelyn Atahualpa
utterances.text: Good morning, everyone.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jocelyn Atahualpa
utterances.text: My name is Jocelyn Atahualpa, and I've been a member of Queens Neighborhoods United since 2014.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jocelyn Atahualpa
utterances.text: I call Corona, Jackson Heights, and Elmhurst my home, and these neighborhoods are overrun with ice.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jocelyn Atahualpa
utterances.text: Many of us living in this part of Queens start our days the same way.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jocelyn Atahualpa
utterances.text: I wake up and check my phone to see where ICE is at, how many cars and agents, and if there are any confirmed abductions.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jocelyn Atahualpa
utterances.text: Throughout the day, I wait to hear if the person abducted was identified and if the family was connected to legal resources.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jocelyn Atahualpa
utterances.text: If there aren't any updates, I anticipate calls from the family or directly from a detention center.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jocelyn Atahualpa
utterances.text: These have been my mornings for over a year.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jocelyn Atahualpa
utterances.text: I wouldn't wish this on anyone.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jocelyn Atahualpa
utterances.text: The violence and trauma we're experiencing at the hands of ICE is unlike anything I've experienced in my entire life.

chapters.summary: Atahualpa says ICE is ravaging her community within a 20-block radius and that NYPD has willingly helped ICE. She describes ICE cars at precincts, crossing guards asking about immigration status, and a mother beaten by ICE while her children became nonverbal.
chapters.title: Atahualpa describes ICE violence and NYPD cooperation

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jocelyn Atahualpa
utterances.text: ICE is ravaging our communities, upending our lives, all within just a 20-block radius.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jocelyn Atahualpa
utterances.text: And it feels like no one in the city cares.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jocelyn Atahualpa
utterances.text: Canal Street happens, Marble Hill happens, and then everyone forgets.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jocelyn Atahualpa
utterances.text: Almost everyone in our part of Queens has either been directly impacted by ICE or knows someone who has.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jocelyn Atahualpa
utterances.text: We are acutely aware of how little this city cares for undocumented.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jocelyn Atahualpa
utterances.text: and how that's made us susceptible to ISIS attacks.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jocelyn Atahualpa
utterances.text: The Thursday following Trump's inauguration was the first time I received a call about a raid in our area.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jocelyn Atahualpa
utterances.text: For most of 2025, we were swarmed by ICE, but it wasn't until later that year that we started feeling the severe physical violence.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jocelyn Atahualpa
utterances.text: From street abductions to violent car raids, the escalations haven't stopped.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jocelyn Atahualpa
utterances.text: To make matters worse, there are several recorded instances of NYPD willingly helping ICE.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jocelyn Atahualpa
utterances.text: ICE cars parked at both the 115th and 110th precinct, even local NYPD crossing guards asking about immigration status and doing ICE's bidding.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jocelyn Atahualpa
utterances.text: Just because ICE hasn't successfully pulled the trigger on us doesn't mean they haven't pointed weapons at our heads.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jocelyn Atahualpa
utterances.text: The violence has been nonstop for over a year now.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jocelyn Atahualpa
utterances.text: Just last weekend, I met a mother who'd been beaten up by ICE.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jocelyn Atahualpa
utterances.text: They put a taser to her head and said, fuck you and your babies.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jocelyn Atahualpa
utterances.text: These babies are three-year-old U.S.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jocelyn Atahualpa
utterances.text: Citizen twins who are now nonverbal.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jocelyn Atahualpa
utterances.text: Ice broke the father's nose and ribs.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jocelyn Atahualpa
utterances.text: He's currently detained and only receiving ibuprofen for his diabetes.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jocelyn Atahualpa
utterances.text: We have reason to believe it was ACS negligence that led to this.

chapters.summary: Atahualpa describes coordinating 5 a.m. ICE watch patrols, door-to-door investigations, and supporting immigrant women after abductions. She says neighbors help with rent, groceries, medicine, childcare, and emotional support, and run a monthly support group.
chapters.title: Atahualpa describes mutual aid and support work

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jocelyn Atahualpa
utterances.text: These past two years, I've coordinated 5 a.m.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jocelyn Atahualpa
utterances.text: Ice watch patrols, led door-to-door investigations to identify abducted neighbors, and cried with countless immigrant women as they pour out their pain following the abduction of a loved one.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jocelyn Atahualpa
utterances.text: You probably can't understand.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jocelyn Atahualpa
utterances.text: and how that feels.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jocelyn Atahualpa
utterances.text: To stand with a stranger in shock following one of their most traumatizing experiences.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jocelyn Atahualpa
utterances.text: It shatters you.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jocelyn Atahualpa
utterances.text: Neighbors like me help with rent, with grocery and medicine, with childcare, and with emotional support that makes us all a bit more bearable.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jocelyn Atahualpa
utterances.text: We help access legal resources and stand with them as they navigate a system designed to isolate them and get rid of them.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jocelyn Atahualpa
utterances.text: We have a monthly support group that's helping us all process the trauma and creating a space for testimony from recently liberated men.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jocelyn Atahualpa
utterances.text: We embroider and talk about the abuse and injustice and who is profiting off these abductions.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jocelyn Atahualpa
utterances.text: We help stabilize rupture families by bringing them together to support one another and learn from each other.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jocelyn Atahualpa
utterances.text: We do all of this because no one else is doing it.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jocelyn Atahualpa
utterances.text: But we know our real campaign is to make sure no one else is taken from our communities.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jocelyn Atahualpa
utterances.text: For the past year, we have been desperately trying to hold on to each other and claw each other back from the jaws of Trump's deportation machine.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jocelyn Atahualpa
utterances.text: And even when we bring someone back home, it still doesn't feel like a true win.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jocelyn Atahualpa
utterances.text: Everyone knows they're living on borrowed time.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jocelyn Atahualpa
utterances.text: We are strongest when we are organized and united.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jocelyn Atahualpa
utterances.text: We know there is a future in which ICE won't dare enter our communities and no one will dare collaborate with ICE, formally, informally, or even by negligence.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jocelyn Atahualpa
utterances.text: This city is full of people who are outraged and want to make this a reality.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jocelyn Atahualpa
utterances.text: We need the city and nonprofits to get behind us.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jocelyn Atahualpa
utterances.text: It's your task as our city's leadership to represent that energy.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jocelyn Atahualpa
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Elsie Encarnación
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: Elsie Encarnación
utterances.text: Before we continue, I just wanted to acknowledge that we've been joined by Councilmember Carmen De La Rosa and Councilmember Chanel Thomas-Henry.

utterances.speaker: Elsie Encarnación
utterances.text: You may go.

chapters.summary: Naima Dahir introduces herself as Advocacy Manager at the Arab American Family Support Center. She says AAFSC serves about 20,000 people yearly, 70% born outside the U.S., and provides legal support as a MOIA-established center.
chapters.title: Naima Dahir introduces Arab American Family Support Center

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Naima Dahir
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Chair and Council and members of the Committee on Immigration.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Naima Dahir
utterances.text: My name is Naima Dahir, and I am the Advocacy Manager at the Arab American Family Support Center, also known as AAFSC.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Naima Dahir
utterances.text: AAFSC serves roughly 20,000 people each year across New York City, 70% of whom are born outside of the United States.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Naima Dahir
utterances.text: We work every day to support immigrant families and ensure they have access to essential social services with safety and dignity.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Naima Dahir
utterances.text: As a MOIA-established legal support center, we also provide free critical legal support to families navigating the immigration legal system.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Naima Dahir
utterances.text: Over the past several months, our staff, many of whom are immigrants themselves, have seen a surge in fear, increased requests in basic assistance, and increased mental health challenges.

chapters.summary: Dahir says mixed-status families are self-deporting and naturalization applications have declined. She describes a pregnant mother whose husband was detained, and how AAFSC helped pay rent, legal costs, and food before he was deported without due process.
chapters.title: Dahir describes family separation case and support

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Naima Dahir
utterances.text: Mixed-status families are increasingly choosing to self-deport rather than risk detention or family separation.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Naima Dahir
utterances.text: We've also seen a sharp decline in community members applying for naturalization.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Naima Dahir
utterances.text: Last year, a month ago,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Naima Dahir
utterances.text: Mother came to us after her husband was detained by ICE.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Naima Dahir
utterances.text: She was left to care for two young children while pregnant with her third.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Naima Dahir
utterances.text: Without our family's primary source of income or knowledge of her husband's whereabouts, she came to us in a time of crisis.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Naima Dahir
utterances.text: And through a coordinated effort with our teams, we were able to pay her overdue rent,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Naima Dahir
utterances.text: cover her legal costs, and put food on the table.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Naima Dahir
utterances.text: Her husband was eventually deported without due process, leaving her as the sole provider and caregiver.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Naima Dahir
utterances.text: Her family continues to face the lasting financial and emotional toll of the separation.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Naima Dahir
utterances.text: Unfortunately, this is not an isolated incident.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Naima Dahir
utterances.text: The lives of so many of the families in our communities have been upended by immigration detention.

chapters.summary: Dahir says the city must ensure its agencies and resources are not used to facilitate federal deportation. AAFSC supports the Cut Ties with ICE package, closing sanctuary loopholes, limiting local cooperation, and requiring judicial warrants.
chapters.title: Dahir calls for closing sanctuary loopholes and supports bills

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Naima Dahir
utterances.text: While the city cannot control federal immigration enforcement, it has an important role to play in protecting immigrant New Yorkers.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Naima Dahir
utterances.text: It can and it must ensure its agencies, resources, and personnel are not used to facilitate or advance federal deportation agenda.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Naima Dahir
utterances.text: For these reasons, AAFSC supports the ties with ICE legislative backage being presented today.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Naima Dahir
utterances.text: We must close loopholes in our sanctuary laws, limit local cooperation with ICE, and prevent individuals from being held beyond their lawful release time without a judicial warrant.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Naima Dahir
utterances.text: These protections are essential to safeguarding due process, maintaining community,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Naima Dahir
utterances.text: trust in ensuring immigrant New Yorkers can access essential services without fear.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Naima Dahir
utterances.text: Thank you for the time and the opportunity to testify today.

utterances.speaker: Elsie Encarnación
utterances.text: Thank you for testifying.

utterances.speaker: Elsie Encarnación
utterances.text: Thank you all for your bravery and what you've had to endure in your communities.

utterances.speaker: Elsie Encarnación
utterances.text: I want to open up if any of the council members have questions for this panel.

chapters.summary: Councilmember Alexa Avilés thanks Assemblymember Cruz for her work and asks for concrete recommendations for the City Council and colleagues. She notes that other officials may lack Cruz's depth of experience.
chapters.title: Avilés asks Cruz for concrete recommendations

utterances.speaker: Alexa Avilés
utterances.text: Assemblymember, thank you so much for your steadfast work in protecting immigrant communities.

utterances.speaker: Alexa Avilés
utterances.text: Could you tell us a little bit more about

utterances.speaker: Alexa Avilés
utterances.text: some of the concrete recommendations that you would like particularly this city council to take, but also

utterances.speaker: Alexa Avilés
utterances.text: our colleagues who are facing the struggle in their communities, often not with the depth of experience that you bring.

utterances.speaker: Alexa Avilés
utterances.text: So thank you.

chapters.summary: Cruz recommends training every staffer on know-your-rights and creating a network among elected officials. She says city and state agencies, especially the Department of Education, need training for all personnel and consequences for policy violations, including NYPD.
chapters.title: Cruz recommends staff training, networks, consequences

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Catalina Cruz
utterances.text: Thank you, Councilmember Aviles.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Catalina Cruz
utterances.text: You know, I first want to highlight that while I get to do some of this work, it's my team that's doing it every single day.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Catalina Cruz
utterances.text: And I think that's the first very basic recommendation that I would have for all of my colleagues, no matter what level of government you're in.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Catalina Cruz
utterances.text: I think every single staffer needs to be trained on know your rights.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Catalina Cruz
utterances.text: And I think we should, frankly, as elected officials, create a network.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Catalina Cruz
utterances.text: And I want to give a shout out to my council member, Janelle Thomas, because between her team and my team and a couple of other colleagues, we manage our little area.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Catalina Cruz
utterances.text: But I think, John,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Catalina Cruz
utterances.text: It's just correct.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Catalina Cruz
utterances.text: It often feels like we are alone in this.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Catalina Cruz
utterances.text: And even if we have amazing volunteers and even if we have elected officials, it's simply not enough because of the sheer number of daily kidnappings that are happening.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Catalina Cruz
utterances.text: We just don't have the capacity.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Catalina Cruz
utterances.text: So capacity building within our offices, training within our offices, but for the city and state agencies, as I mentioned before, with the Department of Education, it is imperative that we provide

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Catalina Cruz
utterances.text: every single person, the lunch lady, the front desk person.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Catalina Cruz
utterances.text: You know, I almost forgot about that when I heard the story of the crossing guard that was asking about immigration status.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Catalina Cruz
utterances.text: I almost forgot about that story.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Catalina Cruz
utterances.text: That should not be happening.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Catalina Cruz
utterances.text: And so we need every single person that touches that system to be trained about the rights of immigrants, their own rights, consequences if they break any of the policies of the city.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Catalina Cruz
utterances.text: And frankly, we need to start implementing those consequences, which takes me back to the first example that I gave, which was the NYPD.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Catalina Cruz
utterances.text: In my conversations with them, they have been very responsive and they have reiterated that there is no cooperation.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Catalina Cruz
utterances.text: There is a big difference between saying it and seeing it.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Catalina Cruz
utterances.text: They're saying there's no cooperation, but what the community is seeing, whether it's on social media, the incident that I described in Jackson Heights earlier in the summer, there was an officer almost smirking on camera while ISIS kidnapping someone behind them.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Catalina Cruz
utterances.text: And so.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Catalina Cruz
utterances.text: You know, part of the job is also we got to shell out a little bit of punishment here.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Catalina Cruz
utterances.text: If someone is breaking the policies that we are saying are in place, then we need to start doing that.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Catalina Cruz
utterances.text: So for me, it's a little bit of training, a little bit of consequences.

chapters.summary: Atahualpa says many mothers become single mothers overnight and need help with housing vouchers. She suggests a relocation program because neighborhoods feel haunted by ICE even when ICE is not there.
chapters.title: Atahualpa suggests housing vouchers and relocation program

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jocelyn Atahualpa
utterances.text: Sorry, you didn't ask me this question, but I have some thoughts.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jocelyn Atahualpa
utterances.text: I think there's a lot of mothers that become single mothers overnight, and they're living haunted by what happened to them.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jocelyn Atahualpa
utterances.text: We would really appreciate facilitation with moves with folks that have vouchers, housing vouchers.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jocelyn Atahualpa
utterances.text: That would really help.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jocelyn Atahualpa
utterances.text: And then just generally maybe creating some sort of relocation program to help us facilitate with these single mothers.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jocelyn Atahualpa
utterances.text: They're living inside a prison in their homes.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jocelyn Atahualpa
utterances.text: All the blocks remind them of what happened.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jocelyn Atahualpa
utterances.text: It's just...

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jocelyn Atahualpa
utterances.text: Our neighborhoods right now feel like they're haunted by ice, even when ice isn't there.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jocelyn Atahualpa
utterances.text: So that would be like a very tangible thing.

chapters.summary: Dahir agrees with Cruz and adds that community-based organizations have built trust and are often the first place families turn. She urges continued investment in culturally responsive community organizations doing the work on the ground.
chapters.title: Dahir urges investment in community-based organizations

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Catalina Cruz
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Catalina Cruz
utterances.text: And please feel free to jump in.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Naima Dahir
utterances.text: I think the only thing that I would add, which I completely agree with you, is that there's so many community-based organizations that are on the ground who've built trust within the community.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Naima Dahir
utterances.text: And so we are kind of like the first person that they come to.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Naima Dahir
utterances.text: So I think continual investment in culturally responsive...

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Naima Dahir
utterances.text: community-based organizations that are really doing this work on the ground is important.

chapters.summary: Avilés says families face imprisonment in their homes and total collapse of income, with first responders raising money for impacted families. She calls for city funds to support real-time mutual aid and accountability throughout the system.
chapters.title: Avilés responds on income collapse and mutual aid

utterances.speaker: Alexa Avilés
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Alexa Avilés
utterances.text: And I would just add, you know, I think what we see is not only families who become imprisoned in their homes, but a total collapse of income, right?

utterances.speaker: Alexa Avilés
utterances.text: And which has fallen onto the hands of first responders in the community to continue to raise money for families impacted, to make sure they are able to stay in homes, to make sure that the kids are receiving what they need.

utterances.speaker: Alexa Avilés
utterances.text: So first and foremost, thank you.

utterances.speaker: Alexa Avilés
utterances.text: For doing that work.

utterances.speaker: Alexa Avilés
utterances.text: And I hope that you are also able to receive care for yourself because dealing with trauma is traumatizing as well.

utterances.speaker: Alexa Avilés
utterances.text: And our city needs to think about how do we set up funds also that can support that real-time mutual aid that is easy and expeditable in addition to these larger policy questions.

utterances.speaker: Alexa Avilés
utterances.text: And Assemblymember, I will say this is a real problem.

utterances.speaker: Alexa Avilés
utterances.text: When the community does not know who keeps them safe, we will continue to have this problem.

utterances.speaker: Alexa Avilés
utterances.text: We need accountability up and down the system.

utterances.speaker: Alexa Avilés
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Elsie Encarnación
utterances.text: Thank you, Chair.

utterances.speaker: Elsie Encarnación
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Elsie Encarnación
utterances.text: Thank you all.

utterances.speaker: Elsie Encarnación
utterances.text: I'm now going to call up the admin to take on their seat.

utterances.speaker: Elsie Encarnación
utterances.text: Thank you, Commissioner, for being here.

utterances.speaker: Elsie Encarnación
utterances.text: And I will turn it over to the committee council to administer the oath before we hear the mayoral administration's testimony.

chapters.summary: Council staff announce the administration panel: Commissioner Faiza Ali from MOIA, Deputy Commissioner Lorena Lucero, and NYPD Deputy Commissioner Michael Gerber. Staff administer the affirmation to tell the truth before testimony begins.
chapters.title: Staff administers affirmation to administration panel

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: Thank you, Chair.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: We will now hear testimony from the administration.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: We will hear from Commissioner Faiza Ali from MOYA, MOYA Deputy Commissioner of Programs and Policy, Lorena Lucero, and NYPD Deputy Commissioner of Legal Matters, Michael Gerber.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: Before we begin, I will administer the affirmation.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: Panelists, please raise your right hand.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: Do you affirm to tell the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth before this committee and to respond honestly to council member questions?

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: You may begin when ready.

chapters.summary: Commissioner Faiza Ali introduces herself as Commissioner of the Mayor's Office of Immigrant Affairs. She thanks the pre-panel witnesses for their bravery in sharing the realities communities face every day.
chapters.title: Commissioner Faiza Ali introduces MOIA and thanks pre-panel

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Faiza Ali
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Faiza Ali
utterances.text: Thank you, Chair and Conor Sion and members of the Committee on Immigration for the opportunity to testify today.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Faiza Ali
utterances.text: My name is Faiza Alin.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Faiza Ali
utterances.text: I'm the Commissioner of the New York City Mayor's Office of Immigrant Affairs.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Faiza Ali
utterances.text: Before I begin, I just want to say thank you to our pre-panel, our Assemblymember Naima and Jocelyn for

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Faiza Ali
utterances.text: their testimony, and I think you said this, Chair, for their bravery in sharing the realities that our communities are experiencing on the ground every day.

chapters.summary: Ali says immigration enforcement has become increasingly aggressive, with ICE killing people and at least 32 dying in custody this year. She describes arrests in neighborhoods, courthouses, and public places, and the fear affecting schools, work, businesses, and medical care.
chapters.title: Ali describes aggressive federal enforcement and impacts

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Faiza Ali
utterances.text: Across the country, the immigration enforcement has become increasingly aggressive with significant consequences for immigrant communities.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Faiza Ali
utterances.text: This year alone, ICE has killed several people during their enforcement.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Faiza Ali
utterances.text: At least 32 people have also died this year in ICE's custody.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Faiza Ali
utterances.text: Across the five boroughs, federal agents are carrying out arrests in residential neighborhoods, on city streets, at immigration courthouses, and in other public places.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Faiza Ali
utterances.text: Subjecting New Yorkers to dangerous conditions in ICE detention and separating families.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Faiza Ali
utterances.text: Enforcement activity is affecting neighborhoods in all five boroughs.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Faiza Ali
utterances.text: The presence of ICE in our communities has left immigrant New Yorkers feeling terrified, anxious, and uncertain.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Faiza Ali
utterances.text: Parents are concerned about sending their children to school.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Faiza Ali
utterances.text: Workers are weighing the risks of going to their jobs.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Faiza Ali
utterances.text: Businesses are seeing a drop in business and visits from immigrant customers.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Faiza Ali
utterances.text: Families are delaying medical care, and some immigrant New Yorkers are even afraid to leave their homes.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Faiza Ali
utterances.text: Several recent incidents have brought the consequences of these enforcement practices into sharp focus.

chapters.summary: Ali cites the Marble Hill shooting of Oscar Belgal, ICE detentions near schools in Corona, and an incident in the Bronx where agents detained a student to draw out her father. She says ICE does not make the city safer.
chapters.title: Ali cites Marble Hill, Corona, Bronx incidents

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Faiza Ali
utterances.text: ISIS shooting.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Faiza Ali
utterances.text: Of Oscar Belgal in Marble Hill last month with his five-year-old child in the backseat on a crowded residential street deeply shook our entire city.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Faiza Ali
utterances.text: In Corona, ICE agents were reported detaining individuals near an elementary school and a high school, raising concerns among students, parents, and school communities.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Faiza Ali
utterances.text: In the Bronx just days later, Moya learned of a reported incident in which federal immigration agents detained a student in an effort to draw her father out of their home.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Faiza Ali
utterances.text: These incidents make clear what New Yorkers have known for a long time.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Faiza Ali
utterances.text: ICE does not make our city safer.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Faiza Ali
utterances.text: Their actions have spread fear, torn families apart, and put lives at risk.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Faiza Ali
utterances.text: There is no place for this kind of violence in our communities, and that is why Mayor Mondani has demanded an end to ICE enforcement in New York City.

chapters.summary: Ali says the federal government is carrying out a mass de-legalization campaign projected to leave 213,000 people in the New York metro area without legal status by the end of 2026. She cites TPS terminations, asylum rule changes, and declining approval rates.
chapters.title: Ali discusses de-legalization and policy changes

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Faiza Ali
utterances.text: As a federal government has supercharged its enforcement operations, it is also carrying out mass

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Faiza Ali
utterances.text: de-legalization campaign that expands the reach of those operations and impacts New Yorkers'livelihoods.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Faiza Ali
utterances.text: According to Forward.us, federal policy changes are projected to leave 213,000 people in the New York metro area without legal status by the end of 2026.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Faiza Ali
utterances.text: Rapidly changing policies, such as the termination of humanitarian protections like TPS for residents of more than a dozen countries,
