utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Faiza Ali
utterances.text: rules changing how asylum cases are decided, and a historic decline in approval rates, to name just a few,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Faiza Ali
utterances.text: have resulted in widespread fear and confusion amongst immigrant communities about what applies to them, what their rights are, and what happens next.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Faiza Ali
utterances.text: The city's responsibility is to stand with affected communities and use every tool within our authority to protect New Yorkers.

chapters.summary: Ali says MOIA connects information on the ground with a coordinated city response. MOIA monitors developments, works with City Hall and the Interagency Response Committee, and communicates with trusted community organizations.
chapters.title: Ali describes MOIA monitoring and interagency response

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Faiza Ali
utterances.text: MOIA plays a central role in that effort by connecting information on the ground with a coordinated city response.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Faiza Ali
utterances.text: Through our ongoing engagement with community organizations, advocates, state partners, and New Yorkers, MOIA has been closely monitoring developments across the city and hearing directly about their impact.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Faiza Ali
utterances.text: Our relationships are critical to understanding where enforcement is occurring, identifying emerging concerns, and coordinating an effective city response.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Faiza Ali
utterances.text: When we learn of enforcement activities taking place, MOIA works with City Hall, the Interagency Response Committee, and our interagency partners to establish the facts, coordinate an appropriate response,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Faiza Ali
utterances.text: response and communicate with trusted community organizations and advocates.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Faiza Ali
utterances.text: In a climate where misinformation can spread quickly, providing accurate and timely information is essential.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Faiza Ali
utterances.text: Our community engagement team also works directly in impacted neighborhoods.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Faiza Ali
utterances.text: Staff share know your rights information, distribute resources, meet with residents and community leaders, and identify immediate needs.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Faiza Ali
utterances.text: Through MOYA's Immigration Legal Support Hotline and a network of legal service providers, we connect individuals and families with legal assistance.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Faiza Ali
utterances.text: We also work with CBOs to support legal clinics, Know Your Rights workshops, and other services.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Faiza Ali
utterances.text: This work continues beyond the immediate incident.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Faiza Ali
utterances.text: MOIA stays in close contact with community partners to understand long-term impacts, to identify gaps in support, and connect families with resources.

chapters.summary: Ali says Mayor Mamdani signed Executive Order 13 to strengthen local laws limiting city participation in federal immigration enforcement. Under EO 13, agencies reviewed policies and protocols to identify gaps and provide clear guidance to city employees.
chapters.title: Ali discusses EO 13 and agency safeguards

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Faiza Ali
utterances.text: The city is also strengthening the safeguards that govern how our own agencies interact with federal immigration authorities.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Faiza Ali
utterances.text: In February, Mayor Mamdani signed Executive Order 13 to strengthen the implementation of local laws that limit or prohibit city agency participation in federal immigration enforcement.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Faiza Ali
utterances.text: Under EO 13, agencies undertook a comprehensive review of policies and protocols related to interactions with federal immigration authorities to identify gaps, to reinforce existing protections, and provide clear

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Faiza Ali
utterances.text: guidance to city employees.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Faiza Ali
utterances.text: This work spans multiple agencies including ACS, DOC, DOP, DSS, and NYPD as well as H&H and New York City Public Schools, both of which who participated voluntarily.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Faiza Ali
utterances.text: The objective is straightforward.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Faiza Ali
utterances.text: City employees must understand their obligations.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Faiza Ali
utterances.text: Agencies must have clear protocols for responding to federal immigration authorities.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Faiza Ali
utterances.text: And the city must protect the privacy of New Yorkers and their access to our facilities and services.

chapters.summary: Ali reports that all audited agencies adopted final policies on access to city property and are posting protocols. She details NYPD's new policies on civil immigration detainers, information requests, property access, and patrol guide rules on immigration enforcement.
chapters.title: Ali reports progress on audits and NYPD policies

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Faiza Ali
utterances.text: We have continued to make progress on the implementation of adopted recommendations since our last hearing.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Faiza Ali
utterances.text: I'm happy to share that all audited agencies have adopted final policies regarding access to non-local law enforcement to city property and are working to post their updated access to property protocols as required by EO 13.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Faiza Ali
utterances.text: Agencies have also made continued progress on their agency-specific

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Faiza Ali
utterances.text: updates to policies and protocols.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Faiza Ali
utterances.text: At ACS, all quality assurance case reviewers have now been trained to alert immigration services and language affairs when they find inappropriate references to a person's immigration status in their case reports.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Faiza Ali
utterances.text: DOHMH has now updated post-incident protocols and is refining the process for notifying appropriate parties about interactions with non-local law enforcement.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Faiza Ali
utterances.text: It has also

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Faiza Ali
utterances.text: developed, posted, and completed its audit of facility signage.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Faiza Ali
utterances.text: The NYPD has now finalized and issued four new policies as part of the adopted recommendations from the 2025 DOI report and the implementation of EO-13.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Faiza Ali
utterances.text: First, the NYPD has memorialized its process for processing and tracking civil immigration detainer requests.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Faiza Ali
utterances.text: Furthermore, the updated guidance on reporting civil immigration detainer requests as a result of the implementation of EO-13 audit recommendations now requires the NYPD

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Faiza Ali
utterances.text: DOC and DOP to submit these reports quarterly.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Faiza Ali
utterances.text: Second, the NYPD has issued new protocols for requests for information from law enforcement agencies unrelated to joint criminal investigations through a task force or the Intelligence and Counterterrorism Bureau.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Faiza Ali
utterances.text: Third, the NYPD has issued an access to a property protocol.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Faiza Ali
utterances.text: Policy that prohibits unauthorized use of non-public areas of its property by external governmental agencies.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Faiza Ali
utterances.text: And finally, the NYPD has issued a new patrol guide policy that reiterates the prohibition on the use of city resources for immigration enforcement.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Faiza Ali
utterances.text: This policy institutionalizes protocols requiring the Communications Division to notify the Operations Division in connection with any 911 calls related to immigrants.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Faiza Ali
utterances.text: matters to ensure the appropriate executive oversight of the department's response.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Faiza Ali
utterances.text: The patrol guide details actions that the officers are required to take when encountering federal immigration enforcement activity,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Faiza Ali
utterances.text: including activating body-worn cameras and ascertaining the identity of federal law enforcement personnel on the scene and establishing a crime scene when possible.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Faiza Ali
utterances.text: The policy also reminds officers of their duty to facilitate First Amendment activity and the procedure to elevate allegations of misconduct, including against federal law enforcement agents.

chapters.summary: Ali says the administration issued guidance on non-local law enforcement access to city property and warned of legal action over ICE's unauthorized use of city-owned lots. She describes a new Parks Department policy for frontline workers.
chapters.title: Ali discusses city property and Parks policy

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Faiza Ali
utterances.text: The administration has also taken steps to address the use of city-owned property for federal immigration enforcement.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Faiza Ali
utterances.text: In June, the administration issued updated guidance and best practices to agencies concerning non-local law enforcement attempts to access city property and lots.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Faiza Ali
utterances.text: Earlier this month, Mayor Mamdani warned that the city would pursue legal action if ICE continues its unauthorized use of city-owned property to stage enforcement operations.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Faiza Ali
utterances.text: Reports of ICE using city-owned lots, including near Van Cortlandt Park in the Bronx and Flushing Meadow Park

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Faiza Ali
utterances.text: in Corona, Queens, are particularly troubling given the proximity these spaces have to residential neighborhoods and places where families gather.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Faiza Ali
utterances.text: Alongside this letter, the Parks Department issued a new policy for frontline workers, which strengthens the procedures that

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Faiza Ali
utterances.text: Parks employees must follow when responding to attempts by non-local law enforcement, including ICE, to access Parks property.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Faiza Ali
utterances.text: This new policy and ongoing training will ensure Parks employees are equipped to protect park spaces for the safe use and enjoyment of all New Yorkers.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Faiza Ali
utterances.text: This administration is committed to working with community leaders and our elected officials to ensure city spaces are safe for immigrant New Yorkers, so we urge individuals who witness any concerning practices to contact MOYA

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Faiza Ali
utterances.text: at askmoya at cityhall.nyc.gov.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Faiza Ali
utterances.text: The city is also engaging private property owners.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Faiza Ali
utterances.text: Following the reported use of a privately owned parking lot as a staging area for enforcement operations in Marble Hill,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Faiza Ali
utterances.text: Mayor Mamdani and more than 100 elected officials from across New York State sent a letter to more than 1,700 parking garage and lot owners.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Faiza Ali
utterances.text: Urging them to not rent, lend, or otherwise make their property available to ICE for its operations.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Faiza Ali
utterances.text: These actions reflect our commitment to protecting New Yorkers while our local laws already place

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Faiza Ali
utterances.text: strong limits on city cooperation with federal immigration enforcement, the current climate demands that we continually assess and strengthen these protections.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Faiza Ali
utterances.text: We must identify gaps, close them, and use every tool available under our local authority

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Faiza Ali
utterances.text: to safeguard New Yorkers and ensure that city agencies and resources are not used to facilitate federal immigration enforcement.

chapters.summary: Ali expresses support for the spirit of Intro 739 and says the administration supports limiting local resources for federal immigration enforcement. She notes the Law Department is reviewing Intros 1077-A and 1078-A and promotes MOIA's expanded legal support hotline.
chapters.title: Ali expresses support for bills and hotline expansion

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Faiza Ali
utterances.text: That is why I am pleased to express our support for the spirit of the legislation being considered today.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Faiza Ali
utterances.text: Introduction 739 sponsored by Councilmember Hanif would require city agencies, contractors, and subcontractors

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Faiza Ali
utterances.text: to train their staff on and publicly post their implementation plans governing interactions and cooperation with non-local law enforcement.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Faiza Ali
utterances.text: Much of this work has already commenced through EO13, and we support efforts to train relevant staff on these critical procedures.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Faiza Ali
utterances.text: Regarding introductions 1077A and 1078A, both sponsored by Chair Encarnacion,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Faiza Ali
utterances.text: would make changes to the local laws regarding civil immigration detainers and the circumstances in which DOC may communicate with federal immigration authorities.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Faiza Ali
utterances.text: The administration supports limiting the use of our local resources, including law enforcement, for assistance with federal immigration enforcement.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Faiza Ali
utterances.text: The law department is reviewing both bills.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Faiza Ali
utterances.text: Before I conclude, I want to remind New Yorkers, as our public advocate did in his remarks,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Faiza Ali
utterances.text: anyone who needs immigration legal help can call MOIA's free, safe, and confidential immigration legal support hotline at 1-800-354-0365.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Faiza Ali
utterances.text: Moya's hotline has also

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Faiza Ali
utterances.text: expanded its hours Monday through Friday, 9 to 8 p.m., and Saturday and Sunday from 9 a.m.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Faiza Ali
utterances.text: To 5 p.m.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Faiza Ali
utterances.text: This moment calls for sustained action, clear accountability, and a city government prepared to meet its responsibility to every New Yorker.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Faiza Ali
utterances.text: We will continue to stand with our immigrant communities, enforce laws and protections, address gaps, and work with our partners to ensure that every person who calls New York City home

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Faiza Ali
utterances.text: can seek help, can go to school, to ensure that every person, regardless of their immigration status, can continue to live in our city and thrive in our city.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Faiza Ali
utterances.text: Our commitment is to protect the dignity and safety of all New Yorkers and ensure that our values are reflected in our actions.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Faiza Ali
utterances.text: Our administration looks forward to work in partnership with the City Council to uphold that commitment.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Faiza Ali
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Elsie Encarnación
utterances.text: Thank you, Commissioner.

utterances.speaker: Elsie Encarnación
utterances.text: Before we get into questions, I would like to allow some time for two of our colleagues to give a statement.

utterances.speaker: Elsie Encarnación
utterances.text: The first will be Carmen De La Rosa, and then followed by Chanel Thomas-Henry.

utterances.speaker: Elsie Encarnación
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: Councilmember Carmen De La Rosa represents Washington Heights, Inwood, and Marble Hill, which she says have become a bullseye for ICE violence. She describes the shooting of Oscar Belgal, detentions, macing, and staging in parking lots.
chapters.title: De La Rosa describes ICE violence in her district

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: Thank you, Chair Encarnacion, for holding this important hearing at an inflection point in our country's immigration enforcement.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: I represent the communities of Washington Heights, Inwood, and Marble Hill, all of which have become a bullseye for ICE proliferation of violence and chaos.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: In my districts, I see...

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: agents fired several shots with an assault rifle into a vehicle where Oscar Bagal and his five-year-old son were sitting.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: They detained Dylan on his way home from school, and they have disappeared several of our neighbors across Washington Heights.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: They maced a neighbor at Inwood Hill Park over the summer.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: And have staged at the Target shopping center and parking lots across Upper Manhattan and the Bronx.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: My community cannot take it anymore, and our communities will not take it anymore.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: This is a rogue agency whose actions destabilize families, scare our children,

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: impact our local economies when business have to shut down as crime scenes and lose their workers for fear.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: And ICE operations, frankly, are not good public safety policy.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: We view them as violence.

chapters.summary: De La Rosa asks how to empower communities when the federal government ignores rights and how to address public perception that NYPD facilitates kidnappings. She says the conversation must go beyond protocols to strategy and communication.
chapters.title: De La Rosa questions sanctuary enforcement and NYPD perception

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: We held countless Know Your Rights canvases and briefings and trainings, but what good are they when the federal government turns its back on our rights?

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: How do we then empower communities, especially in sanctuary cities like ours, to stand up and protect its people in the face of impunity?

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: Today's hearing not only furthers this conversation, but also allows us to have tangible conversations around legislation that bolsters the city's response to collaboration with ICE.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: I must ask, how do we ensure that our communities feel

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: when public perception is that the NYPD is facilitating the kidnappings of our neighbors in our communities.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: While I am grateful to Mayor Mamdani, to Commissioner Ali, and to all of the members of the administration that have really made this a point of priority for our communities, I stand here as someone who represents a community that is crippled

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: by fear.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: We must do more.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: The conversation must go beyond.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: And as a council member, I'm looking forward to understanding the protocols, the procedures, but also the strategy behind how we communicate with New Yorkers that they are indeed safe.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: I look forward to hearing from agencies, from advocates, from everyday New Yorkers on what the path forward must look like.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: We want to ensure that we protect vulnerable New Yorkers who have become the target of federal enforcement.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: We must protect First Amendment rights to protest.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: And we must not feel like we are imprisoned in our own communities at this time.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: I'm looking forward to engaging with all of you in good faith, understanding that the safety of our neighbors means the safety of all of our neighbors.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: Not just the very few, not just the privileged few.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: So I'm looking forward today to having this conversation.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: And I know this is not the last, and I know this is not the first, but I hope that we have a tangible step forward from this hearing on to ensure that the executive orders that have gone into effect and the laws that we have passed are being followed.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: followed to the letter of the law.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: Councilmember Shanel Thomas-Henry represents District 21 in Queens, including Corona, and says three neighbors were taken by ICE in 24 hours. She asks what it says about society when children fear their parents won't come home.
chapters.title: Thomas-Henry describes Corona ICE activity and moral question

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: Thank you, Chair Carnation, not only for holding this very important hearing, but for being a resource and support to me and my district as we continue to battle this attack by ICE on our communities.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: I also want to thank my state colleague, Assemblymember Catalina Cruz, for coming and testifying today about what is happening in our communities.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: I am Councilmember Chanel Thomas-Henry, and I proudly represent the 21st Council District in Queens, which includes Corona.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: Corona has experienced an alarming increase in ICE enforcement activity.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: Just yesterday, our community partners reported that three of our neighbors were taken by ICE within 24 hours.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: And tragically, this is no longer an isolated incident.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: It is becoming our reality.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: But when did enforcing the law become an excuse to abandon our humanity?

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: Because before we can debate immigration policy, we have to confront a fundamental moral question.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: What does it say about us as a society when children are afraid their parents won't come home?

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: When families are torn apart and when simply going about your daily life becomes an act of courage.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: These three neighbors are not immigration enforcement statistics.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: They are three families whose lives have been turned upside down.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: Three households left wondering if their loved ones will ever come home.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: And in Corona and East Elmhurst, these are not distant stories.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: These are our neighbors, our families, our communities.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: We see and feel what immigration enforcement is doing to our neighborhoods.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: My office has helped families whose loved ones were detained without warning.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: We've connected them to legal services, helped navigate complicated cases, and witnessed firsthand how overwhelmed our community partners have become.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: And when we ask why families cannot get help, we hear the same answer, capacity.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: So my question is simple.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: What are we doing to fix that?

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: We cannot tell families they have rights while leaving them without the resources to exercise them.

chapters.summary: Thomas-Henry supports Intros 1077-A and 1078-A to prohibit holding individuals beyond release on civil detainers without judicial warrants. She calls for more legal representation, community partnerships, counseling, and accountability, and says fear will not have the final say.
chapters.title: Thomas-Henry supports bills and calls for resources

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: That's why this package of legislation matters.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: Interest 1077A and 1078 would prohibit the NYPD and Department of Correction from holding individuals

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: beyond their scheduled release solely on civil immigration detainers without judicial warrants.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: Because our local agencies should not become an extension of federal immigration enforcement at the expense of the trust we've worked so hard to build in our communities.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: But legislation alone is not enough.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: We need more legal representation, stronger community partnerships, counseling for families and children, and real accountability about those needs.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: So today I'm calling on my colleagues.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: To advance this legislation and on our city to match these protections with the resources necessary to make them meaningful.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: And I want every immigrant family in District 21 to hear me clearly.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: Fear will not have the final say in our communities.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: We will work to protect you.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: And on a personal note, I just want to say it's been, it's come far too often where I drop my kids off at school and have to respond to ICE enforcement just blocks away.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: Community members, brave community members who are fighting to help save these individuals are being maced in our streets.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: And even this week, I want to thank the admin for the letters that were sent out, but even this week, our parks property parking lots are being used for ICE activity.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: We need help.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: We need help and we need to protect our communities.

utterances.speaker: Elsie Encarnación
utterances.text: Thank you, Council Members.

utterances.speaker: Elsie Encarnación
utterances.text: We are going to begin with questions, and I'm going to go back and forth from NYPD and MOIA because I can't decide on which one I want to go down completely.

chapters.summary: Chair Encarnación asks NYPD how the new ordinances and protocols will be used and rolled out, especially regarding training. She thanks the department for detailing work with Operations Order No. 4.
chapters.title: Chair asks NYPD about new protocols and training rollout

utterances.speaker: Elsie Encarnación
utterances.text: I want to thank you for detailing some of the work that you've done with Operation Order No.

utterances.speaker: Elsie Encarnación
utterances.text: 4 and the updates that you've brought to this.

utterances.speaker: Elsie Encarnación
utterances.text: And so for the NYPD.

utterances.speaker: Elsie Encarnación
utterances.text: How do you see the new ordinances and the new protocol being used?

utterances.speaker: Elsie Encarnación
utterances.text: How do you see it being rolled out, specifically as it pertains to the training related that would be needed for this new order?

chapters.summary: NYPD Deputy Commissioner Michael Gerber explains that Operations Order 4 was a concise 2025 document synthesizing legal obligations. He says it has now become several freestanding policies on civil immigration detainers, information requests, property access, and immigration status inquiries.
chapters.title: Gerber explains Operations Order 4 and new policies

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: So we just to take a step back just for a second, going back to January of 2025, right?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: We anticipated that immigration enforcement was going to change in this country and in the city, and we put out Operations Order 4, right, which was

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: a two-page document meant to synthesize the legal obligations and legal restrictions on NYPD officers.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: By design, it was short, it was concise, simplified in certain respects, because we want to put that out so officers understand in a fundamental way, here are the key principles that are guiding our officers going forward.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: And that operations order actually turns out to be, I think our data shows, like the most read operations order in the department's history, or certainly one of the most read in the department's history.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: You know, what's happened over time, right, over the last almost two years,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: is we've learned, right?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: We've learned from experience.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: We've learned from the DOI report, which was incredibly helpful.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: We've learned from EO13 and the audit that followed from that.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: And as sort of part of that learning experience, what we've done is we've taken that operations order four, and that has now become several different

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: policies.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: I'll just walk the committee through sort of those different policies and how they're functioning and then talk about the training piece.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: So what are the different policies that we have in place?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: So one piece is about civil immigration detainers, right?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: We have not honored a civil immigration detainer in a decade, not one.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: But we wanted to have, still, on paper, clear policy.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: What's the process?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: And so we have a policy now, a freestanding policy, memorializing just that.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: And I should just say, the way that policy works, the bottom line is, before we would honor any immigration detainer, again, we have not done in a decade, but if someone were contemplating doing that, there would have to be numerous approvals, including from an executive in the legal bureau.

chapters.summary: Gerber describes a significant process for external requests for information, including supervisory review, documentation, vetting, and legal bureau approval. He says vague requests receive follow-up questions and every request is reviewed by a legal bureau executive.
chapters.title: Gerber details information request vetting process

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: That's one part.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: A second part is requests for information from outside agencies, right?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: Now, if we are working on a criminal investigation with another agency, including other federal agencies, because these are criminal cases, not enforcement matters, and we have task forces that do that with various federal agencies, not immigration related,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: there is sharing of information, right?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: That's what it means to have a joint investigation.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: But...

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: For any other type of request from outside agencies.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: And it's not just federal.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: Federal, another state, they come to us, they say, hey, we have criminal matter we're working on.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: They say it's a murder investigation.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: Hey, we think you have information relevant to our murder investigation.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: Can you help us?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: We have put in place a very significant process for those kinds of requests.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: Supervisory review, documentation of the request, all sorts of information has to be filled out.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: A vetting process, both on the uniform side and then every single one of those requests has to go to a legal bureau executive.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: We have to approve every single one of those.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: And frankly, to the extent their request is vague in some way, follow-up questions.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: Hey, we don't have enough information here.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: Sometimes it's clear in its face.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: Sometimes it's like, no, no, this is too vague.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: We need to know more.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: So we have now a freestanding policy just for that to channel all those requests across the department.

chapters.summary: Gerber says NYPD has a freestanding policy prohibiting use of department property for immigration enforcement and another prohibiting inquiries about immigration status. He says any officer asking about immigration status commits a flagrant violation that will be investigated by IAB.
chapters.title: Gerber discusses property access, immigration status inquiries, accountability

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: There is now a freestanding policy about access to department property.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: To be clear, we already had, obviously, a rule saying you can't use department property for immigration enforcement.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: But then we have a freestanding policy on that.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: We have a freestanding policy about not inquiring about immigration status.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: And there was a reference to this in the testimony before.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: I want to be very, very clear.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: If there's a member of service who's asking people about their immigration status, that is a flagrant violation of department policy.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: And frankly, if that is referred to us, that will be investigated by IAB.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: If it is substantiated, the consequences for that will be severe.

utterances.speaker: Elsie Encarnación
utterances.text: Is that what should happen?

utterances.speaker: Elsie Encarnación
utterances.text: Should people flag it to?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: That should go.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: And I can tell you with great confidence that will be investigated by IAB.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: And if it is substantiated.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: That's charges and specs, right?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: That is incredibly serious.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: And again, a flagrant violation of our policy.

chapters.summary: Gerber says the general immigration enforcement policy is now codified in the patrol guide and states NYPD does not do immigration enforcement or assist it. He describes 911 call notifications, body-worn cameras, identifying federal agents, and protecting First Amendment activity.
chapters.title: Gerber explains patrol guide immigration enforcement policy

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: And then there's also sort of the general immigration enforcement policy, right?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: And we had that in Operations Order 4.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: We now have it codified in the patrol guide, right?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: It's permanent.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: That's important.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: And that sets out the core principle.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: And the core principle is we do not do immigration enforcement.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: We do not assist.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: We do not help.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: We cannot use city resources, broadly defined, right?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: We cannot do that, period.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: The policy is very clear.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: The policy includes a reference to a practice we've had for a while now, but again, it's important to put it in policy, of any time a 911 call comes in, whoever it comes from,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: that references immigration enforcement in any way, notification process, operations is notified.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: That does several things.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: It ensures that you will have the appropriate executive coverage, right?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: When our cops are being put in incredibly challenging situations,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: terrible situations, you want executives on the scene to help navigate this, and in every one of those cases, call to the legal bureau, right?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: A legal bureau executive getting involved either on the phone or on scene with

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: uniform side executives.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: There are other things in this policy, if I may, just a few things.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: You know, reinforcing, again, these are not new principles, but it's very important to reinforce them in this context in the immigration enforcement policy.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: So, for example,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: Our officers, if they are on scene and there's any kind of immigration enforcement happening, body-worn cameras on.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: They have to do their very best to identify who are these federal agents, right?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: I got to say, we cannot compel the federal agents to tell us who they are, but we can ask, we can inquire.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: We can press on that because we want to know who are we dealing with here?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: Who's here?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: To identification.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: There's obviously in the policy, there's also, for example, a reminder about the critical importance

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: of if in response to immigration enforcement, there's First Amendment activity, right?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: We have to protect that.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: We have to facilitate that.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: So again, some of these things are not, they're not new principles to the department, but putting them in the immigration enforcement policy, I think sends a very strong message.

chapters.summary: Chair Encarnación asks about training and notes that in Oscar's case officers arrived without knowing ICE was on scene. She asks Gerber to address that scenario before discussing training.
chapters.title: Chair asks about training and 911 calls not identifying ICE

utterances.speaker: Elsie Encarnación
utterances.text: I agree.

utterances.speaker: Elsie Encarnación
utterances.text: And

utterances.speaker: Elsie Encarnación
utterances.text: Can you speak to the training piece of it?

utterances.speaker: Elsie Encarnación
utterances.text: And also, before I get to that, you mentioned the 911 calls that mentioned that it is ICE that is on a scene.

utterances.speaker: Elsie Encarnación
utterances.text: But in the case of Oscar, there was no mention you arrived to the scene without understanding that there was ICE on the scene.

utterances.speaker: Elsie Encarnación
utterances.text: Am I correct?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: Elsie Encarnación
utterances.text: So can you talk in that kind of an incidence?

utterances.speaker: Elsie Encarnación
utterances.text: Can you talk a little bit about that and then get to the training piece?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: Yeah, sure.

chapters.summary: Gerber says the policy applies to immigration enforcement regardless of agency, not just ICE. He says if officers discover immigration enforcement on scene, they must notify supervisors, and in Oscar's case escalation happened quickly.
chapters.title: Gerber explains immigration enforcement policy not ICE-specific

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: So, and I should say, it's not, you know, the way, the guidance, and that's actually an important point, I think, both for the 911 policy and for our policies generally.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: It's not...

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: ICE specific.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: It's about immigration enforcement, whoever's doing it.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: Right?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: We have had situations in which, and there was certainly a lot of this in 2025, I think we're seeing less of this in 2026, but still, other federal agencies sometimes getting pulled in, sort of detailed to do immigration enforcement.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: Our policy does not distinguish based on agency, it's about

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: what agents are doing.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: So, right, anytime there's a reference to immigration enforcement in any way, the 911 call

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: Take care has a protocol they follow.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: Now, if immigration enforcement is not referenced, we can't know what we don't know.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: I will say that as part of our policy, and I think this has been true in practice, if patrol officers come on a scene,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: and come to learn or understand, oh, this is somewhat immigration related, they are going to go over the radio and notify their supervisor, right?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: I mean, they are required to do that as per our policy.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: I also think patrol officers understand that they are, you know, this is part of the challenge, right?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: They show up and all of a sudden they discover they're this incredibly fraught, very challenging situation.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: They need to get supervisors involved.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: So in a situation like that,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: Do we know from the initial 911 calls it was immigration related?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: Were executives, both on the uniform side, legal bureau, and otherwise, notified that this was immigration related?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: That happened very quickly because patrol officers were talking over the radio and it got escalated very fast.

chapters.summary: Gerber describes 2025 training for executives, borough commanders, and COs, plus an all-in refresher. He says new policies will require more training, including targeted executive training and eventually training for all 50,000 uniformed members.
chapters.title: Gerber describes training for executives and all officers

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: With regard to training.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: So what we did back in 20, beginning of 2025, we put operations order for the training focus.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: And we push out the policy to everyone.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: But then we did was we did trainings really for executives and also in a targeted way.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: So.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: I did trainings for the senior executives in the department, executives in Intel, executives in the task forces.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: I did trainings for the borough commanders, trainings for groups of COs.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: We then did, I don't have to deal on this exactly, we did when we had an all-in for all our uniform and civilian executives.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: We had an all-in.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: Part of the all-in was essentially a refresher training that I conducted on our policies.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: Now that we've rolled out the new policies, we are going to be doing more training.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: I think part of that is going to mirror what we did back in 2025.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: That is, I think it's very important to have trainings, targeted trainings for executives.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: With a particular focus again on the task forces, on the intel leadership, borough commanders, CEOs, and all that.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: I think the piece that we need to work on is figuring out how to do this, how to do some sort of training for everybody.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: For all uniformed members of service.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: Obviously, we can't just do in-person training for 50,000 members of service overnight.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: We have to think about what that training looks like.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: But that's something I think we're going to want to do.

utterances.speaker: Elsie Encarnación
utterances.text: Yeah, I mean, if we're talking about having to train all of the OE employees, I think they're going to face the same trouble.

chapters.summary: Deputy Commissioner Lorena Lucero says putting policies on paper clarifies law enforcement's role and creates accountability. Chair Encarnación asks what that accountability looks like.
chapters.title: Lucero adds importance of written policies for accountability

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lorena Lucero
utterances.text: And Chair, I just wanted to add just the importance of getting these policies on paper because they not only clarify the role for our law enforcement, but it also creates an opportunity for accountability that has been stressed

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lorena Lucero
utterances.text: from several colleagues on the dais.

utterances.speaker: Elsie Encarnación
utterances.text: And what does that accountability look like?

chapters.summary: Gerber says allegations of sanctuary law violations go to IAB for significant investigation. He cites a DOI finding of a detective who violated sanctuary law and was removed from a task force, had computer access limited, and faced charges and specs.
chapters.title: Chair asks about accountability pipeline; Gerber cites DOI case

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: So anytime we have an allegation of any sort of a violation of the sanctuary city laws, violation of our policy in connection with those laws, that's going to IAB.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: There's going to be a significant investigation.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: I'll give you an example.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: I think it's an important one.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: DOI in its report, which was a very positive report in many ways, found one instance of a detective and a member of the task force who had violated sanctuary city law and violated our policies.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: And the consequences were swift and severe.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: That individual was, and we worked collaboratively with the OI to look into what had happened.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: But the consequences were removed from the task force.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: Computer access was severely limited.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: Facing charges and specs, charges and specifications.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: That's the most serious type of internal discipline that we have.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: That case is still pending.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: And so it's not yet been resolved.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: But in terms of NYPD discipline, that's as serious as it gets.

utterances.speaker: Elsie Encarnación
utterances.text: And do you have information on how many folks are in kind of like that accountability pipeline?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: I mean, we definitely can provide the council with some data on that.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: I do want to distinguish, right?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: I want to be careful about this, right?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: Because there are times, to be blunt, there are times when allegations come in.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: substantiated and there's very significant disciplinary fallout.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: There also are times when allegations are made and they turn out sometimes not to be accurate.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: That does happen.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: There are times allegations are made and they're not supported by evidence.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: And everyone, right, has due process rights.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: So

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: And I do want to be sensitive to that, right?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: Like it's not just the allegation is made and therefore the person engaged in misconduct.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: It has to be an investigation.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: That's fair.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: Yeah, that's part of the pipeline.

utterances.speaker: Elsie Encarnación
utterances.text: That's fair.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: But we certainly can provide some data in terms of certainly like, certainly about, you know, for example, cases where there has been substantiation and charges have been brought.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: We definitely can provide that to the committee.

utterances.speaker: Elsie Encarnación
utterances.text: We love that.

utterances.speaker: Elsie Encarnación
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: Chair Encarnación says observers saw NYPD clear a path for ICE vehicles on the night of Oscar's shooting. She asks Gerber how the new policies address perceptions of NYPD collaboration with ICE.
chapters.title: Chair asks about NYPD clearing path for ICE at Marble Hill

utterances.speaker: Elsie Encarnación
utterances.text: And then on the night of the shooting of Oscar, there were a number of observers that say that they saw the NYPD clear the path for ICE vehicles.

utterances.speaker: Elsie Encarnación
utterances.text: This also came up in the testimony of Assemblymember Catalina Cruz, where we were talking about perception and kind of like this perception of collaboration or some kind of.

utterances.speaker: Elsie Encarnación
utterances.text: Information sharing or helping of from the NYPD to ICE.

utterances.speaker: Elsie Encarnación
utterances.text: So can you speak a little bit about how you interpret Operation Order 4 and this new iteration and how you see that helping clear this up?

chapters.summary: Gerber says the hospital entrance had to remain clear for ambulances and employees. He says ICE asked to coordinate their exit and NYPD refused, but officers moved protesters out of the way to prevent people from being hurt or killed.
chapters.title: Gerber explains hospital access and refusal to coordinate ICE exit

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: Sure, sure.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: There are a few pieces to that, and I want to address all of them.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: First of all, in terms of the space outside Allen Pavilion, outside of the hospital there, it's a hospital entrance.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: And it's one way in, one way out about hospital, which I think is extremely important.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: I want to emphasize that.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: The entrance to a hospital cannot be blocked.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: For obvious reasons, ambulances have to be able to get in.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: Hospital employees have to be able to get in.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: And so there was a time that night and I can go through the sequence of events if it's helpful.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: But we did come to a point where there were individuals in the street blocking the street.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: We need to keep the street clear for access.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: To the hospital, right?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: And that is totally appropriate and we stand by that.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: We cannot have the entrance to a hospital blocked.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: Now, in terms of when the ICE vehicles came out, because there came a time a little before 11 when a whole group of what were clearly ICE vehicles came out of the hospital.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: I want to say that before that happened, earlier in the evening, someone from the ice team approached us, approached me, and asked if we could coordinate their exit.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: And we refused.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: We said no.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: They asked.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: They're allowed to ask.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: We said, absolutely not.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: We cannot do that.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: Period.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: I think it's important.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: When they came out, and we did not know when they were coming out, but they did come out, there were a small number of people, not a lot.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: But there were a few who essentially jumped in front of the cars or trying to block the cars.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: And it is true that NYPD officers move those individuals out of the way.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: In doing that, that is not the NYPD coordinating with ICE or assisting ICE.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: What that is, is trying to prevent people from getting hurt or getting killed.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: And what I would say to individuals who believe that we shouldn't have done that, my question would be, if we're not doing that, if we just walk away,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: How does that story end?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: How does that story end?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: We've seen what happens in other cities.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: And that ends with people getting hurt, sometimes people getting killed.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: And the most basic obligation of an NYPD officer is to protect human life.

chapters.summary: Chair Encarnación asks whether anyone moved from in front of cars was arrested. Gerber says five civilians were arrested that night, but not the individuals moved from in front of the vehicles.
chapters.title: Chair asks about arrests; Gerber says five civilians, not those moved

utterances.speaker: Elsie Encarnación
utterances.text: Were any of those people arrested, by the way, that were stopped from, that were peeled off the car?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: Elsie Encarnación
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: Elsie Encarnación
utterances.text: How many people were arrested that night that were civilians?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: In total, five.

utterances.speaker: Elsie Encarnación
utterances.text: In total, five.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: But it was not, I'm quite certain it's not any of those individuals.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: And I just do want to, I do want to go back to this point.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: I understand the optics piece.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: I understand the concerns that have been raised.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: I get it.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: Totally understood.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: And to the extent that that

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: erodes trust in NYPD officers, that's a terrible thing.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: And if that is going to cause people to hesitate, for example, to report a crime or to speak to an NYPD officer, that's terrible.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: But it is also the case that if we walk away, I genuinely believe that the alternative is people getting hurt, people getting killed, and we can't let that happen.

chapters.summary: Chair Encarnación notes Assemblymember Cruz described another incident without the same one-way hospital parameters. She asks how Gerber sees that case as similar.
chapters.title: Chair asks about other incident without hospital parameters

utterances.speaker: Elsie Encarnación
utterances.text: Now, that was the case, as you said, for this particular one way in, one way out.

utterances.speaker: Elsie Encarnación
utterances.text: The assembly member mentioned another incident that does not have the same parameters as the hospital.

utterances.speaker: Elsie Encarnación
utterances.text: And so in those cases.

utterances.speaker: Elsie Encarnación
utterances.text: How do you see that being the same as this particular case?

chapters.summary: Gerber says there are infinite factual permutations and officers often walk into unknown situations. He says in the other incident NYPD officers were standing between protesters and ICE agents out of concern for human life.
chapters.title: Gerber explains varied facts and NYPD standing between protesters and ICE

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: So the challenge here, and it is a real challenge, and I want to acknowledge it, is that there's an infinite number of different permutations of facts.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: That's the truth of it.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: And our patrol officers are put.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: Time and again in this terrible position, right?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: They're responding to scenes.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: They don't know what they're walking into precisely because we don't coordinate with ICE.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: They don't know even what's happening when they arrive.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: And our approach, what I think is the right approach, is to have a set of principles, principles memorialized in policy.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: And then as soon as possible, as soon as humanly possible, to get executives on scene, to get lawyers on the phone or on scene.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: I do want to say that what ends up happening in the real world is sometimes things are happening within a matter of minutes.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: You have random patrol officers dealing with terrible situations none of their making, and there isn't time to get an executive on scene.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: There isn't an opportunity for a legal consultation.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: And then each case becomes different.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: I'm not, I think I know which incident was being referred to before.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: I don't think that was actually, if it's what I'm remembering, I don't think that was clearing a path for ICE or anything like that.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: I do think it was, I do think it was NYPD officers standing between protesters and ICE agents.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: And again, where that's coming from, that is coming from a concern for human life, the concern for not wanting to have a situation in which protesters are being hurt or worse.

chapters.summary: Chair Encarnación cites public reporting that HSI agents investigated and canvassed the scene after the shooting. She asks Gerber to describe NYPD involvement with HSI on October 8.
chapters.title: Chair asks about HSI investigation after shooting

utterances.speaker: Elsie Encarnación
utterances.text: I'm going to move on because I know that other council members will touch on this topic again.

utterances.speaker: Elsie Encarnación
utterances.text: But in the...

utterances.speaker: Elsie Encarnación
utterances.text: Public reporting, it reflects that HSI agents investigated and canvassed the scene following that shooting.

utterances.speaker: Elsie Encarnación
utterances.text: Protesters reportedly witnessed NYPD officers speaking with those HSI agents at the protest and at the hospital.

utterances.speaker: Elsie Encarnación
utterances.text: Could you describe?

utterances.speaker: Elsie Encarnación
utterances.text: Any NYPD involvement with HSI on that incident, including any investigatory work that took place on October 8th?

chapters.summary: Gerber says NYPD secured the scene, preserved evidence, and was notified that FBI and HSI would take custody of evidence and the investigation. He says conversations with federal supervisors were about transferring crime scene evidence and were appropriate.
chapters.title: Gerber explains crime scene preservation and federal takeover

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: So,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: Again, there are a few different pieces to that.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: So after the shooting at Marble Hill, there was a period of time where NYPD, you know, we secured the scene, put up

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: crime scene tape, put up cones, identified ballistics.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: We wanted to make sure, obviously, that any evidence was preserved.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: We were notified early on that evening that federal agents, federal agencies, both the FBI and HSI, were coming in to take custody of the evidence and to

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: take over the investigation.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: I want to be clear on that.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: They weren't asking.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: They were telling, and they have the authority to do that.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: And that is, I will say, what happens anytime you have a federal agent discharging a firearm.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: And so what we did, I think, again, I think this was the right thing to do.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: We obviously did not want to have a situation where we caused in any way any evidence to be compromised.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: So we maintained.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: That crime scene until federal agents arrived and took custody of the evidence and processed the evidence.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: In doing that, we certainly had conversations.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: I had conversations with

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: supervisors from the FBI, from HSI, U.S.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: Marshals also there.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: Those were conversations about the transfer of crime scene evidence and the like.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: That's totally appropriate.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: There's nothing wrong with that.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: And then, you know, to the extent there were any conversations at the hospital, I mean, for example, like I said, outside the hospital,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: one of the federal agents came up to me and asked if it would be possible to coordinate their exit.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: And I said no.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: Again, there's nothing wrong with that conversation.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: They are allowed to ask, and I think my response was the right one.

chapters.summary: Chair Encarnación asks whether the city knows how much taxpayer money is used to detain individuals for federal immigration enforcement. MOIA says it does not have that information handy.
chapters.title: Chair asks about taxpayer cost of immigration detention

utterances.speaker: Elsie Encarnación
utterances.text: I'm going to go off outside of October 8th because I'm sure we'll get to it later.

utterances.speaker: Elsie Encarnación
utterances.text: I do want to talk about Intro 1077A.

utterances.speaker: Elsie Encarnación
utterances.text: And does the city know how much taxpayer money is currently being used to detain individuals for exclusive purposes of federal immigration enforcement?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Faiza Ali
utterances.text: I don't know if that's for everybody, but we don't have that handy.

utterances.speaker: Elsie Encarnación
utterances.text: Anyone that can answer, if they can.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Faiza Ali
utterances.text: I don't know if you have it.

chapters.summary: Gerber says NYPD detains no one for immigration enforcement and has not honored an immigration detainer in a decade. He explains Intro 1077-A would remove the 48-hour hold provision, consistent with the Francis case.
chapters.title: Gerber says NYPD detains no one for immigration enforcement; Francis case

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: I can take some on that.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: If I, certainly I can tell you from the PD side, we detain no one for immigration enforcement.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
