utterances.text: Again, we have not, I just want to emphasize this again.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: It has been a decade since we honored a,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: immigration detainer.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: And I also want to emphasize, I think this maybe, Chair, goes to your question, you know, 1077A amends city law so that we cannot hold someone

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: for 48 hours essentially pending a judicial warrant, right?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: The way the city law is written now in certain circumstances, certain triggers, we'd say, oh, the PD should hold this person for 48 hours so that federal authorities can go get a judicial warrant.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: But years ago, in a case called Francis, a second department case, second department said,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: that essentially in that type of context, right, state police officers or state police officers,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: in New York State do not have the authority to hold individuals absent judicial warrant.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: They can't hold individuals for immigration enforcement.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: Right?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: And we've been following that law for years.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: So it's going to be very, very clear.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: We have not had situations where, I mean, since Francis, where we were holding people pending the receipt of some warrant, right?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: Under state law, we can't do that.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: So the answer to your question, at least from the PD side, is who are we, you know, cost of holding people for immigration enforcement?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: Zero, because we're not doing that at all.

chapters.summary: Chair Encarnación asks whether NYPD adopted the EO 13 recommendation to disaggregate civil immigration detainers by conviction status and terrorist screening database match. Gerber says yes and that reporting is current.
chapters.title: Chair asks about EO 13 disaggregated detainer reporting

utterances.speaker: Elsie Encarnación
utterances.text: And can you confirm whether you've adopted the EO-13 recommendation to disaggregate the number of civil immigration detainers locked by conviction status and a possible match to the federal terrorist screening database?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: Yes, we have done that.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: We are current on the reporting.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: We are doing it consonant with the revised guidance from the EO-13 audit.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: Again, every time we report on this, it's always the same.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: There's some number of detainers, and then how many were honored?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: Zero.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: It's always zero.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: But yes, to the extent there's additional reporting breakdown that was recommended under the EO-13 audit, we have totally adopted that.

utterances.speaker: Elsie Encarnación
utterances.text: Okay, thank you.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Faiza Ali
utterances.text: If you would just allow me, because I think I understood your question a bit broader, but just to reiterate here, $0.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Faiza Ali
utterances.text: are put in because we do not honor civil immigration detainers without a judicial warrant.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Faiza Ali
utterances.text: So I just wanted to clarify that because I think when I heard that, I heard a bit, a broader question.

chapters.summary: Chair Encarnación asks MOIA about its role in implementing city detainer laws and its contact with NYPD regarding immigrants in custody. Ali says MOIA serves as a coordinating and oversight body and receives quarterly detainer reports from DOC.
chapters.title: Chair asks MOIA role in detainer laws and DOC communication

utterances.speaker: Elsie Encarnación
utterances.text: Actually, maybe you guys can help me understand the role that MOIA plays in the implementation of the city detainers laws.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Faiza Ali
utterances.text: Yes, Chair.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Faiza Ali
utterances.text: Samoya, as you know, we serve as a coordinating body across the administration.

utterances.speaker: Elsie Encarnación
utterances.text: Can you bring the mic a little bit closer to you?

utterances.speaker: Elsie Encarnación
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Faiza Ali
utterances.text: We serve as a, we have an oversight body in regards to the detainer laws.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Faiza Ali
utterances.text: We've been playing a more central role along with the IRC and the role that we play there.

utterances.speaker: Elsie Encarnación
utterances.text: And what kind of contact does MOIA have with NYPD in relation to immigrants in department custody?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lorena Lucero
utterances.text: Through our work via the IRC, we work really closely with all city agencies, all audited agencies, including the NYPD.

utterances.speaker: Elsie Encarnación
utterances.text: And are you informed if DLC decides to notify and transfer immigrants to ICE?

utterances.speaker: Elsie Encarnación
utterances.text: You being Moya.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Faiza Ali
utterances.text: Yes, through the quarterly detainer reports that we receive from DOC.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Faiza Ali
utterances.text: And those same reports are sent to the chief counsel, the mayor, and city hall.

utterances.speaker: Elsie Encarnación
utterances.text: Gotcha.

utterances.speaker: Elsie Encarnación
utterances.text: So do you review communication between DOC and ICE?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Faiza Ali
utterances.text: So, again, part of the work that we're doing via the RIC is, and through the EO-13 that we've talked about in the last hearing, we are conducting an email audit of those communications, and that's part of the review that we're doing right now.

utterances.speaker: Elsie Encarnación
utterances.text: And how often does that happen?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lorena Lucero
utterances.text: The audit will be completed by the end of the year, but in general, IRC is meeting with DOC and other agencies regularly.

utterances.speaker: Elsie Encarnación
utterances.text: More than quarterly?

utterances.speaker: Elsie Encarnación
utterances.text: Yeah, more regularly.

utterances.speaker: Elsie Encarnación
utterances.text: More regularly than that?

utterances.speaker: Elsie Encarnación
utterances.text: Okay.

chapters.summary: Chair Encarnación asks whether MOIA helped shape the new Parks Department policy. Lucero says Parks was part of EO 13 work on access to property, and Ali says the policy helps prevent city spaces from being used for immigration enforcement.
chapters.title: Chair asks about Parks policy and MOIA support

utterances.speaker: Elsie Encarnación
utterances.text: I did want to talk about parks because it came up in one of the pre-panel conversations.

utterances.speaker: Elsie Encarnación
utterances.text: Did MOYA help shape the new policy around the new city parks department policy?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lorena Lucero
utterances.text: Yes, so the broader and ongoing work that we're doing, again, part of the executive order, EO 13, parks was part of that.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lorena Lucero
utterances.text: So, yes, we were working with parks and all other agencies to complete revisions on access to property.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Faiza Ali
utterances.text: And Chair, we recognize the importance of ensuring that New York City Parks employees and contractors have the protocols to follow when non-local law enforcement, including ICE, attempts to access parks property.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Faiza Ali
utterances.text: These procedures really help ensure that city spaces are not being used to stage or carry out immigration enforcement operations in a way that is inconsistent with our laws and our policy.

utterances.speaker: Elsie Encarnación
utterances.text: Okay.

chapters.summary: Chair Encarnación asks whether NYPD supports the legislation. Gerber says yes, and Chair Encarnación says it is good to hear before turning to Councilmember Joseph.
chapters.title: Chair asks NYPD support for bills; Gerber says yes

utterances.speaker: Elsie Encarnación
utterances.text: And before I turn it over to my council colleagues, in your opening statement and testimony, you mentioned that you were in support of the legislation that is being proposed today.

utterances.speaker: Elsie Encarnación
utterances.text: Is that the same for you on your end, on the NYPD end?

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: Elsie Encarnación
utterances.text: Good to hear.

utterances.speaker: Elsie Encarnación
utterances.text: Great.

utterances.speaker: Elsie Encarnación
utterances.text: I will now take questions from Council Member Joseph, followed by Aviles.

chapters.summary: Councilmember Rita Joseph says three million immigrants call New York City home and all are living in fear. She describes ICE taking Roberto Lamour from Flatbush and the Haitian community's loss of TPS, and supports Resolution 729.
chapters.title: Joseph makes statement on Haitian and immigrant fear

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: Thank you, Chair.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: I just want to make a statement before I start with my questioning.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: Three million immigrants call New York City home.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: They come from Dominican Republic, China, Mexico, Ecuador, and Venezuela right here.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: All of them are living in fear.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: In my district, that fear has a name.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: On October 3rd, ICE agents...

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: Came to Roberto Lamour's home on Lenox Road in Flatbush.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: His neighbors say the agents claim to be NYPD to get inside.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: Roberto's a Haitian father with no criminal record.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: Today, he's in Mississippi, more than 1,000 miles away from his wife and young daughter.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: Our Haitian community is hurting more than ever.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: 5,440,000 Haitians have lost TPS across the city.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: I shot a Dominican father in Marble Hill with his five-year-old in a car.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: Children as young as 11 are standing alone in immigration courts.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: With a lawyer, immigrants are far more likely to win their case to keep their families together.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: That's why I'm really proud to sponsor Reso 729, which calls on Albany to pass the Build Act.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: Roberto Lamar belongs at home in Flatbush.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: Every immigrant, New Yorkers deserve a fighting chance.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: And I do have two questions.

chapters.summary: Joseph asks what oversight mechanisms NYPD has to ensure officers comply with sanctuary policies and restrictions on ICE cooperation. She asks about internal audits, investigations, and disciplinary actions for improper facilitation.
chapters.title: Joseph asks NYPD about sanctuary compliance oversight

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: Commissioner, always good to see you.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: What specific oversight mechanism does NYPD have in place to ensure officers, department personnel are complying with New York City sanctuary policies and restrictions on cooperation with ICE?

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: Has the department conducted any internal audits, investigation into potential violation, and what disciplinary or corrective action have been taken when officers improperly facilitate federal agent enforcements?

chapters.summary: Gerber says NYPD audited 2025 communications involving task force officers, reviewing tens of thousands of emails. Some cases were referred to IAB, some were unsubstantiated, some substantiated, and some charges and specs are pending.
chapters.title: Gerber describes audit and IAB referrals

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: So we did an audit.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: This year, looking at communications in 2025, involving all the task force officers,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: reviewed, frankly, tens of thousands of emails and pages and communications.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: Coming out of that,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: There were a number of cases or instances that we refer to IAB.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: And I want to be clear, you know, in some of those instances, IAB investigated and it was nothing, right?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: Because we err on the side of caution.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: Sometimes you see an email, you're like, I'm not sure what this is.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: It might be fine.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: It might not be.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: Want IAB to take that and look at it.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: So in some cases, there were cases that were not substantiated.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: There were a number that were substantiated.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: There were a number of pending cases, charges and specs cases against.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: members of service.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: And again, we will provide data to the committee in terms of that.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: I do want to emphasize again that several of those cases are still pending and open, so unresolved.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: But our plan is to do another audit again in the new year.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: Again, for this exact purpose, we want to make sure that people are following the rules, following the law, and if they're not, the consequences will be severe.

chapters.summary: Joseph asks for a detailed accounting of NYPD interactions with ICE over the past year, including information sharing and transfers. She asks what safeguards ensure cooperation is legally permissible.
chapters.title: Joseph asks about NYPD-ICE interactions and safeguards

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: Thank you for that.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: Can NYPD provide detailed accounting of its interaction with ICE over the past year, including instances of information sharing, assistance with enforcement operations, responding to ICE requests, or facilitating transfer of individuals into federal custody?

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: What safeguards are in place to ensure that any cooperation is legally permissible and does not violate city policy?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: So I guess there are a few pieces to that.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: I mean, one is, you know, we do the quarterly reporting now, both with regard to immigration detainers, but also, and this was a fair critique from DOI in terms of making sure we were doing this the right way, right?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: So we're reporting quarterly basically on...

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: Other than detainers, just like requests that we get in connection with immigration enforcement from any quarter.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: It could be ICE, it could be some other federal agency.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: So that is tracked.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: We actually have a whole system in place now where all those requests, if they come in, get channeled to operations.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: That allows us to have a...

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: single repository so that we can report out on a quarterly basis.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: So on the data piece of that, that's going out quarterly.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: Now, what we've done policy-wise is to put all these checks in place so that

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: even frankly requests that on their face don't seem to be immigration related get vetted.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: So again, like in the request for information context,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: Again, if it's part of a joint investigation, we know what it is.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: Our detectives are working on the case.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: What's the much more sensitive piece, right, is these external requests where we're not on the case, where someone from a different jurisdiction, again, it could be federal, it could be state.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: A different state says, hey, I've got this investigation, NYPD, I think you have relevant information.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: Will you help me?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: And look, we, of course, if there's a serious criminal investigation, we want to assist with that, but we have to vet that.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: And so we have now this whole system documented every time, a form filled out every time, supervisory review every time, legal bureau executive review every single time.

chapters.summary: Joseph asks how many requests have come before NYPD. Gerber says he does not have an exact number but he and legal bureau colleagues receive multiple requests per day to vet, mostly for criminal investigations.
chapters.title: Joseph asks how many requests; Gerber says multiple daily

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: And how many have come before you?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: So I don't have the number exactly.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: I will say this.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: These are not immigration requests.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: You just request generally.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: And how many are immigration if you know?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: So, so.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: I would just say that myself and some of my other

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: colleagues in the legal bureau, executives in the legal bureau, we get multiple requests per day to vet.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: Again, I want to be clear, the vast majority of those are totally fine, right?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: Helping with a murder investigation, helping with a drug trafficking investigation, fine.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lorena Lucero
utterances.text: Can I jump in here, Council Member?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lorena Lucero
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lorena Lucero
utterances.text: Part of the role that MOIA has under Local Law 228, those reports are publicly available and include not only the NYPD but other agencies.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lorena Lucero
utterances.text: And it documents incidents in which non-local law enforcement seek information or assistance.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lorena Lucero
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lorena Lucero
utterances.text: Again, from city agencies.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lorena Lucero
utterances.text: So that's available on MOIA's website.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lorena Lucero
utterances.text: Happy to share that information with you after the hearing.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lorena Lucero
utterances.text: I don't have it handy.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lorena Lucero
utterances.text: Yeah, that would be awesome.

chapters.summary: Joseph asks what data NYPD collects and publicly reports on ICE interactions. Gerber says NYPD now reports quarterly on detainers and other requests, including descriptions and responses, and says requests for immigration assistance are denied.
chapters.title: Joseph asks about public reporting; Gerber describes quarterly reports

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: That would be awesome.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: Chair, I just have two more questions, if that's okay.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: What data does NYPD currently collect, publicly report regarding its interaction with ICE, and will the department commit to providing regular transparent reporting to the council on these interactions, including

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: nature of requests received, whether they were granted or denied, and the legal basis for any cooperation?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: So as my colleague was saying, we put that out.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: It's quarterly now.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: And again, there are two reports that go out to the council and to the public.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: One, detainers, and the other is everything else.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: And that's tracked and it goes through for each one.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: It'll say there was a request.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: It's a brief description of what transpired.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: And then it will say,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: Our response was, I will tell you time and again, there was a request for assistance with immigration enforcement.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: Documents were not provided.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: Right?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: We're not doing that.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: Okay, because the optics look different to the public.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: I understand that.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: So we want to make sure that.

chapters.summary: Joseph asks how many unaccompanied minors have been in court without representation. Lucero says she does not have the number handy, and Joseph says there are about 1,400 in the system, asking how many live in New York City.
chapters.title: Joseph asks MOIA about unaccompanied minors

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: Moya, a question for you.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: Unaccompanied minors, 11-year-olds standing in court defending themselves, how many young people have been in court unaccompanied?

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: Can you give us a number?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lorena Lucero
utterances.text: I don't have that number handy, but we have been tracking not only the number of people and even when there were some of those federal cuts,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lorena Lucero
utterances.text: partnering with the state to provide support, given some of the changes that were happening on the contractual side with the feds.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lorena Lucero
utterances.text: So it's an issue that we're looking at closely.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lorena Lucero
utterances.text: I don't have the number handy.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: We have about 1,400 unaccompanied minors in the system.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: So is the city coordinating that funding, and how many of those children live in New York City?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Faiza Ali
utterances.text: About half, I believe, live in New York City.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Faiza Ali
utterances.text: And, Councilmember, I can sense pain in your voice because you and I have talked about the challenges facing our unaccompanied children.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Faiza Ali
utterances.text: In fact, we've sat in courtrooms and seen children go before a judge without an attorney.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Faiza Ali
utterances.text: As my colleague has stated, we worked really closely with the governor's team and our state partners in ensuring that we have the legal resources and the funding that goes to organizations that represent these children.

utterances.speaker: Elsie Encarnación
utterances.text: And Councilmember Joseph, we have to move on, okay?

utterances.speaker: Elsie Encarnación
utterances.text: I'll come second round.

utterances.speaker: Elsie Encarnación
utterances.text: Second round.

utterances.speaker: Elsie Encarnación
utterances.text: And then we will also, just for everyone's edification, we will be having a hearing on unaccompanied minors specifically in the new year.

utterances.speaker: Elsie Encarnación
utterances.text: So please have some numbers ready for us when we discuss that.

utterances.speaker: Elsie Encarnación
utterances.text: Next up is Avila, followed by De La Rosa.

chapters.summary: Councilmember Avilés says public defenders have reviewed body cam footage where NYPD assisted ICE with home arrests. She asks under what circumstances NYPD would accompany ICE to make an arrest in someone's home.
chapters.title: Avilés asks NYPD about accompanying ICE home arrests

utterances.speaker: Alexa Avilés
utterances.text: A lot of questions, not enough time.

utterances.speaker: Alexa Avilés
utterances.text: I'd like to start with NYPD.

utterances.speaker: Alexa Avilés
utterances.text: So public defenders have testified in the past that they have reviewed body cam footage where NYPD was assisting with ICE and home arrests.

utterances.speaker: Alexa Avilés
utterances.text: Under what circumstances, if any, would NYPD accompany ICE?

utterances.speaker: Alexa Avilés
utterances.text: To make an arrest in someone's home.

chapters.summary: Gerber says NYPD should never accompany ICE for immigration enforcement. He explains that officers sometimes respond to 911 calls and discover ICE operations, or work with federal agents on criminal matters that are misperceived as immigration enforcement.
chapters.title: Gerber says NYPD never accompanies ICE; explains misunderstandings

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: So if we are talking about immigration enforcement, civil immigration enforcement, or immigration enforcement really in any form, no, never.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: Our officers, our detectives should never

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: be, for example, executing some sort of operation in connection with immigration enforcement.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: And frankly, again, any instance like that should be referred to us so IAB can look into it.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: I do want to make two points on this because sometimes what happens is there's just a genuine misunderstanding as to what's happening.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: So sometimes there are instances where...

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: ICE is doing what it does.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: There's some 911 call that comes in.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: Cops respond having no idea it's an ICE operation, right?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: We've had situations, for example, where a 911 call comes in, says, hey, there are these people standing outside someone's door.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: They're banging.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: I'm not sure what's happening.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: They seem armed.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: And our cops will race over there and discover that this is an ICE enforcement operation.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: So you can imagine a visual, right?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: Our cops are there standing in that doorway, standing next to ICE agents.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: I can easily see why someone might say, oh, see, that's PD and ICE working together.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: It's not what happened at all.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: It's our cops walking into something that they have no idea what it's about.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: The other thing I will say is sometimes what we see.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: Is there are instances where our detectives quite properly are working on a criminal matter, doing criminal enforcement with federal agents, not related to immigration enforcement,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: But that is sometimes misperceived as immigration enforcement.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: And I understand why.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: You know, the people, they see federal agents, particularly in certain communities, they see federal agents doing enforcement.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: And given everyone's experience, they assume, oh, this is civil immigration enforcement.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: Turns out, actually, it is a criminal matter and totally appropriate.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: But again, if there are instances of any member of the

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: service participating in some sort of immigration enforcement action that is outrageous, that is barred by policy, that is barred by city law, and we would want to have that referral so that IAB can look at it.

chapters.summary: Avilés cites the Kevin Servita Rocha case from February 2024, where his door was broken down and family confined. She asks how NYPD ensures body-worn camera footage is preserved and accessible to the public, not just NYPD.
chapters.title: Avilés cites Kevin Servita Rocha case and asks about body cam preservation

utterances.speaker: Alexa Avilés
utterances.text: Yeah, and the case that I'm referring to in particular is Kevin Servita Rocha in February 2024, who also came before the council.

utterances.speaker: Alexa Avilés
utterances.text: This was widely also reported.

utterances.speaker: Alexa Avilés
utterances.text: In the news where his door was broken down and prevented the family, including his young children, from leaving their apartment for several days.

utterances.speaker: Alexa Avilés
utterances.text: I'd like to know in terms of the new policy of the body-worn cameras, how do we ensure that the footage

utterances.speaker: Alexa Avilés
utterances.text: is not simply in the hands of NYPD, but that there is a directive that requires mandatory preservation and referring the footage outside of just the NYPD.

utterances.speaker: Alexa Avilés
utterances.text: Because you asked me, that is publicly funded footage and should be accessible to the public when we need it, not after it gets curated by the NYPD.

utterances.speaker: Alexa Avilés
utterances.text: So how can we make sure that this footage is preserved and given to the public?

utterances.speaker: Alexa Avilés
utterances.text: When it's required.

chapters.summary: Gerber says body-worn camera footage is preserved for years under normal rules and can be provided to investigating agencies. He says the police commissioner can release footage in the public interest and cites fast release after the Marble Hill shooting.
chapters.title: Gerber explains body-worn camera preservation and release

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: So I would say a few things on that.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: I mean, body-worn camera footage just generally is preserved for a substantial period of time.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: And there are certain preservation rules.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: I don't have them all handy here.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: But, you know, normal course, that footage will be there for some number of years.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: And that's absent any sort of effort to preserve it, just normal course of this preservation.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: I will say, we...

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: To the extent you have any investigating agency, state or federal, that wants that footage, we will provide it, right?

utterances.speaker: Alexa Avilés
utterances.text: Will you provide it immediately?

utterances.speaker: Alexa Avilés
utterances.text: Because what we've seen as a matter of practice is the footage comes out months before, months later.

utterances.speaker: Alexa Avilés
utterances.text: If not years later.

utterances.speaker: Alexa Avilés
utterances.text: Like, it's an indeterminate time of holding things under the guise of its investigation.

utterances.speaker: Alexa Avilés
utterances.text: It's all public materials from my perspective.

utterances.speaker: Alexa Avilés
utterances.text: So what I'd love to hear is we will guarantee that the public is able, we can release it to the parties of the public

utterances.speaker: Alexa Avilés
utterances.text: within a very rapid amount of time so that not only the police investigations can do what they want, but the public can also do what it needs to do with this footage.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: And I will say, obviously, we have a policy about release of body-worn camera footage.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: The police commissioner in any situation in which he determines that it's in the public interest to release body-worn camera footage can do so.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: And, Councilmember, I would say I think in a number of recent instances where there was body-worn camera footage, for example, in connection with the Marble Hill shooting, we had that body-worn camera footage out incredibly fast.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: It was within maybe a day or two.

utterances.speaker: Alexa Avilés
utterances.text: I might be scarred by the past.

chapters.summary: Avilés confirms NYPD supports Intro 1077-A. MOIA says it supports the spirit of the bills and is reviewing with the Law Department, and Avilés says she looks forward to full support.
chapters.title: Avilés confirms NYPD support for 1077A; MOIA reviewing

utterances.speaker: Alexa Avilés
utterances.text: Just one quick question.

utterances.speaker: Alexa Avilés
utterances.text: In terms of, I just wanted to make sure, so in terms of the department, you are here in support of 1077A.

utterances.speaker: Alexa Avilés
utterances.text: I just want to make sure I didn't miss that.

utterances.speaker: Alexa Avilés
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: Alexa Avilés
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lorena Lucero
utterances.text: Be very clear, 100%.

utterances.speaker: Alexa Avilés
Alexa Avilés
utterances.text: And I just wanted to be clear from Waya, you are in support of 1077A as well.

utterances.speaker: Alexa Avilés
utterances.text: We are in support of the spirit of the bills.

utterances.speaker: Alexa Avilés
utterances.text: We are currently reviewing with the law department.

utterances.speaker: Alexa Avilés
utterances.text: And as the bills go through the legislative process, are looking forward to our communication with the council.

utterances.speaker: Alexa Avilés
utterances.text: Okay, we look forward to you being fully supportive of the bills.

utterances.speaker: Alexa Avilés
utterances.text: Thank you, Chair.

utterances.speaker: Elsie Encarnación
utterances.text: Thank you, Councilmember De La Rosa, followed by Brewer.

utterances.speaker: Elsie Encarnación
utterances.text: And I'd also like to acknowledge that we were joined by CM Christian.

chapters.summary: De La Rosa says she witnessed October 8 herself and asks Gerber to acknowledge that past NYPD actions cause mistrust in communities like hers. She cites a case where Commissioner Tisch reversed a guilty finding against an officer.
chapters.title: De La Rosa asks Gerber to acknowledge community mistrust

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: Thank you, Chair.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: October 8th, going back to that date, I was there.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: So none of the things that I'm saying, I was told by anybody else, are things that I witnessed with my own two eyes.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: I want to say, first of all, and I want to ask you, do you acknowledge that past actions by the NYPD would cause mistrust in communities like mine?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: I certainly agree that there have been, that there are communities where there are issues in terms of trust with the NYPD, and we have to do everything we can to build trust in those communities.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: I agree 100%.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: Specifically speaking, under Commissioner Tisch, one of my constituents who was killed by an NYPD officer.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: And your deputy of trials, Maldonado, found the cop guilty.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: Commissioner Tisch reversed that decision.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: You acknowledge that?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: I'm aware of the case, yes.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: You're aware of the case.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: And so when the NYPD is in my community, it is not a far-fetched idea that there would be mistrust.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: With that agency being deployed in communities like ours, especially under a police commissioner who came in as a reformer and has failed to deliver justice for families like Alan Felice's family.

chapters.summary: De La Rosa says she asked Gerber on October 8 what was happening and was told NYPD was investigating the shooting. She asks whether NYPD was investigating or preserving the scene, and later asks why officers allowed ICE agents to flee.
chapters.title: De La Rosa recounts October 8 scene and asks about NYPD role

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: So I put that there because it is important when we go back to the night of October 8th.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: That night, when we arrived at the scene, I specifically asked you, what's happening here?

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: You said, we are investigating the shooting.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: And I said, okay.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: And the congresswoman-elect who was there asked a follow-up question to the investigation.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: You've testified today that you were there securing the scene to make sure that evidence wasn't tampered with and that things were preserved.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: Were you investigating the shooting or were you preserving the scene?

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: A crime scene.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: So a few things.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: Council member, we talked a number of times that evening.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: My memory of the conversation is a little bit different.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: But what I want to be clear about is, and I want to answer your question.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: Early on, right, we were doing things as we would in any situation, securing the scene, making sure evidence was not lost, right, preserving Argus camera video.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: As we would in any situation, right, where there's been a shooting in New York City, we're taking those initial steps.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: Early on, and I just be honest, I do not recall the timing related to our conversation and the call that we got from the FBI.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: But early on that evening, the FBI informed us, and again, they weren't asking, they were telling, that the FBI and HSI were coming in to take over the crime scene.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: And so once that happened, again, that did shift how we were doing things, right?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: It's okay, they're about to come in.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: We're going to keep this secure until they arrive.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: So then what was the NYPD's role once they arrived?

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: Because what I witnessed with my eyes was your officers allowing the ICE agents to flee the community.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: If there was a shooting that happened and the shooter was on the scene, I would think that the NYPD would try to pursue the shooter, would try to have some sort of process to speak.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: to that shooter.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: With my eyes, I witnessed police officers and ICE agents who were now dressed in different clothing all of a sudden leaving the scene.

chapters.summary: Gerber says some ICE agents were in the vicinity but not the ones involved in the shooting. He says NYPD told them to leave and made calls to ensure they left, and directed one ICE agent out of the crime scene area.
chapters.title: Gerber says ICE agents were told to leave crime scene

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: So a few things on that.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: So first,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: When you were there, when you arrived, and I think I was there when you first arrived.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: I believe I was.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: Um,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: There were some ICE agents in the vicinity.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: I do not think that those were the agents involved in the shooting.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: There were other ICE agents there.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: They were sort of like...

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: Hanging out there.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: And I want to tell you that we told them they had to leave.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: And we made some calls because we needed them to leave.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: It was wildly inappropriate in my view for them to just be hanging out there and standing around there.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: We wanted them to leave and they did.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: So I think that was appropriate on our end in terms of how we handled that.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: We shouldn't, we're securing a crime scene.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: You shouldn't have just ICE agents sort of standing around there.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: And when they were walking to their cars, were they not escorted by police officers?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: So there was one instance, right, where there was somebody who, I think it was the other way,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: There was an ICE agent who at some point was, I'm not sure what happened there, was walking through the crowd, like into the sort of crime scene area.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: He walked through the crowd, sort of just emerged.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: We had no idea who this guy was or what he was doing there.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: We weren't going to allow him to just stay in that area.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: And we sort of, you know, basically directed him to leave, which he did.

chapters.summary: Gerber says initial patrol officers focused on saving Oscar Belgal's life and getting an ambulance. He says NYPD had no authority to detain ICE agents and wanted them out of Marble Hill, but De La Rosa challenges the perception of officers escorting ICE to their cars.
chapters.title: Gerber explains officers saved Belgal and did not arrest ICE

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: I want to come back to your broader question, though, if I may.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: About the arrest point, right?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: Now, again, I want to be clear that our initial patrol officers, when they arrived, right, first of all, they were doing one thing and one thing only, and it was the right thing, which is saving Mr.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: Belgal's life.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: I got to say, right, they show up on scene.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: They don't know what this is.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: They have no idea, you know, how we got here.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: But what they have in front of them is Mr.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: Belgal in cuffs, in ice custody, shot.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: And we acknowledge that.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: And that's what they did, right?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: Ambulance.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: Where's the ambulance?

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: Yes, we acknowledge that.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: And they probably saved his life.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: We acknowledge that.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: But as to the broader point, you know, in terms of, I think what you're really getting at, I think, is, you know, why aren't we seeing NYPD officers, you know, putting ICE agents in cuffs?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: I sort of, that's the sense.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: I didn't ask that question.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: I asked why were you all allowing them to safely enter their vehicles and flee the scene?

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: Why were you all allowing that to happen?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: Councilmember, just to be clear, those ICE agents who are standing there, we have no authority.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: So then why are you getting involved?

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: Let them walk to their car on their own accord.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: We have no authority to detain them.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: We wanted them out of there.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: For reasons I think you can appreciate, we did not want ICE agents just like hanging around in Marble Hill.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: Okay, but do you understand the perception for my community when your officers are walking ICE agents, whether they're one of the ones that shot or not, whether they were the ones that were staging in Target or not, to their cars for safety?

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: Who are you protecting?

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: Are you protecting my community or are you protecting the ICE officers?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: So, Councilor, to be clear, my recollection, at least what I saw, is a little different than what you're describing.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: I think it was totally appropriate and, in fact, necessary for us to have those ICE agents leave.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: Because if we had allowed those ICE agents to just, like, stay there, hanging out at a crime scene, I'm pretty sure I'd be hearing rightly from you that it was outrageous.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: There were ICE agents standing around as we were securing a crime.

chapters.summary: De La Rosa says she saw NYPD use barricades as weapons, push people into a pen, and throw the congresswoman-elect to the ground. She asks why the hospital area was not secured earlier and how that was a safety protocol.
chapters.title: De La Rosa challenges NYPD barricade and protest response

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: We disagree with your process.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: I have a few more questions.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Chair, and I know that it's over time, but I do have to ask these questions.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: This happened in my district, so I'm asking for you to allow me to ask my questions.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: First of all, I just want to say about what happened in front of the hospital.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: It is one thing, and we had this conversation on the ground.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: It is one thing, and I understand it, for you to say, hey, we have to make sure that ICE officers, for example, don't go crazy here and start running people over with their cars and all of that.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: But what I witnessed was the NYPD.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: Many community affairs officers that were there that I actually know and have a good relationship with in my district, using the barricades as weapons to push people into a pen situation.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: Our congresswoman-elect was thrown to the ground, okay, in an effort to make a road and an exit.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: Strategy for any vehicle, and I understand ambulances as well, but for vehicles entering and exiting the hospital area.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: When you all knew that there were 90 people, 150 people, and growing a few blocks away on Marble Hill that were going to come down the hill to the hospital.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: Why wasn't the area around the hospital secured before people got there if the goal was to make sure that safety was in place?

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: How is it safe to take barricades and push them?

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: on people and throw people to the ground.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: How is that a safety protocol?

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: I saw people stepped on.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: I saw people pushed to the ground.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: I saw cars basically almost run people over.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: What is the safety in that action?

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: And how do you expect us to not feel assaulted?

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: By the police.

chapters.summary: Gerber says NYPD initially had few barriers and did not want to escalate. After a vehicle was swarmed and attacked, NYPD moved people and later put up barriers to keep the hospital entrance clear, resulting in five arrests.
chapters.title: Gerber describes barriers, vehicle swarming, and five arrests

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: So a few points on that.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: Early on in the evening, and you were there.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: I was there.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: Early on in the evening, we had a few barriers up, not that many.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: There were protesters across the street on Broadway.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: There were protesters on sort of the island there on Broadway.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: And, you know, you had people occasionally stepping into the street, looking in cars.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: It was not an ideal situation.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: We very deliberately did not want to escalate matters.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: We did not want to put up more barriers unnecessarily.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: What ended up happening was one of our vehicles came out of the hospital.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: People then, I think protesters mistakenly believed it was an ICE vehicle, swarmed the vehicle, attacked the vehicle, banging on the vehicle, jumping in front of the vehicle.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: It was incredibly dangerous.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: We ended up having to move people to the side.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: We did not make arrests in connection with that, but it was frankly a dangerous situation.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: At that point, we did not want that to happen again.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: We also had at that point a lot of people in the street blocking the entrance to the hospital.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: And again, one way in, one way out.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: We can't have the entrance blocked for ambulances and otherwise.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: We then put up additional barriers not to interfere with first moment activity.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: It was to prevent people from being in the roadway and blocking the entrance to the hospital, blocking, say, ambulances from getting in or out, or not to have a repeat of what happened just a few minutes earlier.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: Now, I do, I want to bracket the push of Congresswoman Alex Chevalier.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: And the neighbors, not just her, everybody.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: I'm trying to answer your question.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: I want to bracket that piece of it.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: IAB has that matter.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: It is under active investigation.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: And I'm not going to speak to that.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: It would not be appropriate for me to speak to that while the investigation is pending.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: But otherwise, we put up barriers.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: And this is where you and I, I think, just disagree.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: Because what I saw was different than what you saw.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: They weren't pushing people with barricades.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: What I saw was actually mostly it went smoothly.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: And there was a small number of individuals who were.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: are actually not our cops, individuals, pushing on the barriers against the cops to prevent them from locking them together and pushing, using the barriers as weapons, pushing against the cops.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: That's what I saw.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: And the cops didn't push the barriers back.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: And the cops, the cops were working to try to put the barriers in place.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: We ended up making five arrests.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: There were five arrests.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: The barriers were put in place.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: And then the protest continued.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: That's what I saw.

chapters.summary: De La Rosa asks Gerber to explain what happened when ICE vehicles left the hospital after he said NYPD refused to coordinate their exit. Gerber says officers moved protesters out of the way to prevent people from being hurt or killed.
chapters.title: De La Rosa asks why ICE vehicles left safely; Gerber says to prevent harm

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: So just my last question, because I'm running out of time.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: You said that when the officer, when ICE asked you if you would coordinate their exit, you said no.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: So explain to me then what happened when the ICE vehicles left the hospital.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: So there came a moment when all of a sudden you saw this, like, I think it was five or six.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: Cars sort of pulled out.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: It's the SUV.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: I think it was clear to everyone in that moment, oh, these must be the ICE vehicles.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: They started to drive away.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: There was a small number of, I don't think it was a lot, there were a few protesters who

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: essentially moved, were attempting to or were in front of the cars, NYPD officers moved them out of the way.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: And they did that not in coordination with ICE, not to assist with immigration enforcement.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: They did it to ensure that people were not hurt or killed.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: And again, we have seen what happens in other cities.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: The idea that we should have just let them stand in front of that group of ICE vehicles, we'll just, whatever happens, happens.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: That would be an abdication of our responsibility to keep people safe, to prevent people from getting hurt or killed.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: That's what those cops were doing in that moment.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: Gently.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: They gently moved my neighbors out of the way.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: So gently.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: Okay.

chapters.summary: De La Rosa says NYPD's actions did not come across as public safety and urges better real-time communication with communities during incidents. She says the lack of communication worsened distrust instead of letting residents appreciate life-saving work.
chapters.title: De La Rosa urges real-time communication with community

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: Yes, that was the last question.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: I just want to say to you that, in my opinion, although you all were trying to protect public safety, that is not what comes across.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: And I implore you to find a way to communicate clearly to New Yorkers what NYPD's role is when these incidents are happening.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: Not just at the end of the night when the police commissioner comes down to read people's rap sheets at the end of an incident.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: As the deputy commissioner that was on site, someone should have had the ability to communicate with my community.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: what was happening, what the NYPD's role was there, and maybe we would not have seen such an aggressive response to what you all were doing.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: But because it was a moment of tense,

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: Tension and rage, it created a situation where the trust continued to be lost instead of a moment where New Yorkers could have appreciated the life-saving work that the NYPD did in order to preserve Oscar's life.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: So there has to be a communications piece when something is happening live.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: In communities so that we can understand the difference between a police force that is helping ICE agents kidnap our neighbors and flee scenes and the preservation of public safety.

utterances.speaker: Elsie Encarnación
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Elsie Encarnación
utterances.text: Councilmember Brewer, followed by Thomas Henry.

chapters.summary: Councilmember Gale Brewer asks how NYPD will manage future ICE situations so Marble Hill is not repeated. She says ICE agents are not professional and that this is the number one issue for many communities.
chapters.title: Brewer asks how to prevent future Marble Hill incidents

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: My question is to follow up on Councilmember De La Rosa's.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: How are you going to do that in the future?

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: I have a horrible feeling this is not going to be the only incident.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Marble Hill is not going to be the only situation.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: And I know you have all good intentions, and I also know that you don't want the cops to be arrested as part of any kind of federal situation.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: That's what we don't want.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: That's not fair to them.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: It's not fair to the city.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: And to be honest with you, they're professional, and the ICE agents are not.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: They're goons, in my opinion.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: And in fact, I know that's their training.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Some of them would never qualify for public service.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: any way, shape, or form.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: So my question is, how can we manage this in the future so what happened in Marble Hill is not in the future?

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: It's hard, but that is what we need.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: It's the number one issue for so many communities.

chapters.summary: Gerber says ICE comes in, does what it does, and leaves NYPD to deal with the fallout. He says real-time communication is hard because situations are chaotic and NYPD does not coordinate with ICE, so it cannot plan.
chapters.title: Gerber says ICE actions out of NYPD control; communication hard

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: So two points on that.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: I mean, one.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: One is that the challenge here, right, and Councilmember, you just said it, these situations, the way they begin, right, the way we had that whole Marble Hill incident to begin with, right, is out of our control.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: And that's part of the challenge here, right?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: ICE comes in, they do what they do, they leave.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: And then NYPD officers are left to deal with the fallout.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: We've seen that time and again.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: And Marble Hill is the most recent.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: And obviously, it's a singular incident.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: But we see this time and again.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: They do what they do.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: They leave.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: NYPD deals with the fallout.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: I think the question is, from a communications perspective,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: How can we better communicate in real time and otherwise why we're doing what we're doing?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: I will say, look, it's very hard, right?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: We're sitting here in this council room.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: In the moment, particularly outside the hospital that night,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: There wasn't like, this wasn't an organized protest with a single leader where we can sort of

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: In many other contexts, you have somebody who organized a protest.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: We're talking to them.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: We're having back and forth.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: We're trying to figure this out and make sure things go smoothly.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: That's not what you had that night.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: It wasn't like, oh, if we could just talk to this one person.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: There was a lot of rage.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: It was incredibly fraught.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: And so it's, you know, it is one thing to say we want to find better ways to communicate why we're doing what we're doing.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: We do.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: What that means in the moment is very hard to say.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: And also, and part of the challenge here, again, is precisely because we don't coordinate with ICE, we don't know what they're doing and when they're doing it, we're not in a position to plan, right?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: So, right?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: All of a sudden, the ICE vehicles are coming out.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: It's happening now, right?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: There's no planning.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: It's not like, okay, in half an hour, X is going to happen.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: Hey, let's sort of game this out.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: And that's part of the challenge, too, in that moment.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: In that moment, all of a sudden, the ICE vehicles are coming out.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: All of a sudden, there's someone, you know, or a few people jumping in front of those vehicles.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: The cops are doing what they need to do to preserve human life.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: You know, how to communicate better about that, I think is a real challenge.

chapters.summary: Brewer suggests having two or three well-known officers serve as mediators during ICE situations. She asks how the new community safety plan would have changed the Marble Hill response.
chapters.title: Brewer suggests community mediators and asks about new protest plan

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Okay, but it's something to work on.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: I'm no expert, but if I was in charge, I would find that every time,
