utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: an ICE situation exists, I would have two or three cops who are well known to the community to be good mediators, either yourself, not as a police officer, but figuring out who that two or three people person is, have them there,

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: known obviously to the community because they're there so often, and have them be some kind of a

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: discussioner.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: I don't know, but that's what I would look toward because this is going to happen over and over until we get rid of you know who in the White House.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: So that's my question.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: And then finally, I would just say, what is the plan for if there is a new community

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: division if it happens, I don't know if it will, how would that have been any different or you think it would have still been the same situation because it was so last minute?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: No, so it actually goes to your prior question.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: How would things have been different under the new plan, sort of protest plan that was just released?

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Announced by the mayor.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: That's gone into effect, but yes, go ahead.

chapters.summary: Gerber says SRG was not deployed at Marble Hill or the hospital. Under the new plan, the Office of Community Safety would have civilians in dialogue with protesters and a new FAST team within Community Affairs.
chapters.title: Gerber says SRG not deployed; new FAST team and Office of Community Safety

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: So a few points on that.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: I mean, first, I do want to be clear, SRG was not deployed.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: Correct, I know.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: Not at Marble Hill, not at the hospital.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: So that wouldn't make a difference.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: But I think under the new approach, what you would see, you'd see from the Office of Community Safety, civilians in dialogue with protesters.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: You would also see, and this goes to your point, Councilmember,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: members

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: of community affairs from this new FAST team.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: And community affairs, of course, already does lots of dialogue, but they would be focused on that and specialize in that.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: So in that respect, it would be different.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: Okay, thank you, Madam Chair.

utterances.speaker: Elsie Encarnación
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Elsie Encarnación
utterances.text: Thomas Henry, followed by Krishna.

chapters.summary: Thomas-Henry says an ICE vehicle was parked outside a precinct for 20 minutes and another drove into a police parking lot. She asks how new policies will protect New Yorkers when Flushing Meadows Corona Park is understaffed.
chapters.title: Thomas-Henry describes ICE vehicles at precincts and parks understaffing

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: I want to start by saying some of the distrust with NYPD is, although is the appearance of coordination.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: I want to say this week alone, I had a ICE vehicle parked outside of one of my precincts for 20 minutes and the precinct wasn't even aware.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: Community had to notify them and investigate what was happening.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: We had another incident with a precinct, Councilmember Krishnan and I, where ICE vehicle drove into the police parking lot and sat for several minutes.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: So it's repeated incidents of...

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: Blatantly being unaware or what is perceived to not care that these ICE agents are basically trampling over our city with no type of protections or anything in place.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: But what I want to say is there's a number of policies that you've mentioned that have been rolled out, particularly the one with parks, because the Flushing Meadows Corona Park where they are staging is woefully understaffed currently.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: So how do we imagine that these policies will actually protect New Yorkers in real time when we don't have the resources in place now to adequately service?

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: these city assets.

chapters.summary: Ali says the Parks Department rolled out policy updates and MOIA is in ongoing conversations about resources through EO 13. She says city property should not be used for civil immigration enforcement and asks that incidents be flagged to the IRC.
chapters.title: Ali responds on Parks policy and resources

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Faiza Ali
utterances.text: Councilmember, thank you for that question.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Faiza Ali
utterances.text: And, you know, we have talked a little bit about some of the staging that has happened.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Faiza Ali
utterances.text: It has led to, you know, some advocacy and policy changes on our end.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Faiza Ali
utterances.text: And so we were pleased when the Parks Department rolled out their policy updates.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Faiza Ali
utterances.text: With respect to resources, I mean, this is something that we are in ongoing conversations with all of our agencies as part of our Executive Order 13 audit process.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Faiza Ali
utterances.text: This is something that we're in conversation with.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Faiza Ali
utterances.text: But our policies are crystal clear that our facilities, our city-owned property, should not be used to facilitate civil immigration enforcement.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Faiza Ali
utterances.text: And to the incidents that you have laid out today, and I heard some confirmations from another council member on the dais, those incidents should be flagged to whether it's

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Faiza Ali
utterances.text: the members of the NYPD, but can be flagged to any member of the Interagency Response Committee, including MOIA.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lorena Lucero
utterances.text: If I may add, our mayor also reiterated this through a letter and a communication on November 2nd to ICE and use of city-owned lots by ICE, indicating that it is unauthorized.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lorena Lucero
utterances.text: If unauthorized, we will take legal action, and it's part of the work that the commissioner laid out.

chapters.summary: Thomas-Henry asks whether the city has taken legal action since the mayor's letter, noting ICE has returned to the park several times. Ali says it is helpful for elected officials and community members to flag incidents for documentation.
chapters.title: Thomas-Henry asks if legal action taken; Ali asks for incident reports

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: Have we taken any legal action?

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: Because since that letter, they've been at that park several times.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Faiza Ali
utterances.text: Councilmember, it is helpful for any members.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Faiza Ali
utterances.text: elected officials and community members to flag those incidents so we have documentation of that.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: Okay.

chapters.summary: Thomas-Henry says it is disheartening that after almost two years NYPD and DOE have not had proper training. She asks when protecting and informing communities will become a priority.
chapters.title: Thomas-Henry asks about training priority

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: Second question.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: I guess it's disheartening, to say the least, that from a training perspective, one, that we're almost two years and both NYPD and agencies like DOE have not had proper training.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: And even training at a high level, the executives aren't on the street, like, doing the work.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: So at what point in time, and I just mentioned, we have so many czars that I can't even count or keep up with.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: At what point in time are we going to make this a priority?

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: Where we're focusing on protecting, informing our neighborhood communities, protecting our communities, and actually enforcing against when our civil liberties are taken.

chapters.summary: Gerber says training is a priority and he personally trained executives across the department. Lucero says DOE virtual mandated training for principals was completed in October and school safety training was completed in September.
chapters.title: Gerber says training is priority; Lucero details DOE training

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: Councilmember, I just want to emphasize that this is very much a priority.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: We have put a tremendous amount of time and effort and thought into this.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: We had operations order.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: For out in January of 2025.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: I personally undertook the training of executives across the department.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: I think that is absolutely critical.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: And I just, and we said this earlier, in these situations, which are fraught and difficult, we need to get executives on scene and involved.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: And I think we've actually, I think what we have

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: done with this is very much made it a part of the culture of the department that people know anything immigration related, anything immigration related, red flag, calling an executive, getting legal on the phone.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: I think we have done that.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: Can we do more?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: A hundred percent.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: Are we going to do more?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: A hundred percent.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: But it has definitely been a priority.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lorena Lucero
utterances.text: On the Department of Education, training has been completed.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lorena Lucero
utterances.text: The virtual mandated training from principals has been completed in October, and we continue to provide that as needed.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lorena Lucero
utterances.text: On the school safety training, that was completed in September.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lorena Lucero
utterances.text: And then as well, we are working with unions to expand mandated trainings to other school-based staff.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lorena Lucero
utterances.text: Those are some type lines that I have from the work that we're doing with the department.

chapters.summary: Thomas-Henry asks whether New York coordinated with other major cities and what happens when someone is kidnapped on the way to school. Lucero says MOIA has spoken with Los Angeles and Chicago about programs to walk kids to and from school.
chapters.title: Thomas-Henry asks about coordination with other cities and school kidnapping response

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: Before my time, oh, can I put it?

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: Just to double that, New York wasn't the first city that saw this.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: Was there any coordination with any other major municipalities to prepare New York?

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: And in an instance where someone is kidnapped on the way to taking their child to school, what do all the interagency task force, what happens next?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lorena Lucero
utterances.text: Part of the work that we have done, and thank you for raising that, just to elevate some of the coordination work that we have, we do do with other cities, particularly with Los Angeles and Chicago.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lorena Lucero
utterances.text: We have been speaking to them in connections in some of the programs that they have to walk to kids.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lorena Lucero
utterances.text: to and from schools, and it's part of some of the work that we have.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lorena Lucero
utterances.text: I don't have anything more formal than that in regards to some of the work, but again, we're working with the Department of Education and the IRC

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lorena Lucero
utterances.text: to do more formal work on this particular issue because we understand it as being something that is of need to communities at large.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: Councilmember Krishna.

chapters.summary: Councilmember Shekar Krishnan says he wants to focus on per se violations of sanctuary laws even without city intent. He describes ICE staging in a school parking lot and asks how the administration prevents unauthorized use of city property.
chapters.title: Krishnan asks about per se sanctuary violations and city property use

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: Thank you, Chair and Carnation, for this really important hearing today, and thank you all for your testimony.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: I have a few different questions, and we've talked a lot about, we know our sanctuary laws in the city are strong on paper, as long as they're enforced, and there's a lot of conversation and discussion to be had about making sure the city is complying and the agencies are complying.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: What I want to talk about taking a step back is both Councilmember Thomas Henry and I are alarmed every day by the presence of ICE in our communities.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: Terrifying, not even just the individuals they're going after, but terrifying families, so many neighbors beyond whatever the operation may be.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: And we're seeing things on the ground that are raising questions for us.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: And so what I want to focus on today is not so much the city's compliance and where things stand with sanctuary laws, but the instances where there can be violations of the sanctuary laws,

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: even without the city's intent, what I would call per se violations of the sanctuary laws, whether or not the city is aware of it or intends it.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: And here's what I mean.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: I'll give you each of these different examples.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: and I want to go through it.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: The first one was there was a school in my district where ICE staged an operation out of the school parking lot on a weekend.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: The chancellor and I spoke about it directly.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: The school was not aware of it, but we picked up on it after the fact.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: In instances like that, where there are city parking lots,

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: where without the knowledge of a city agency, but it's open and ICE comes into stage and operation, how is the administration, how is MOIA thinking about those instances where city property has been used

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: without the knowledge of the city?

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: How do we take preventative measures to stop that from happening?

chapters.summary: Ali says incidents should be flagged to the IRC, including MOIA, so they can be documented and addressed. She says Queens, especially Elmhurst and Corona, has been the epicenter and MOIA works with community organizations on outreach.
chapters.title: Ali responds on flagging incidents and outreach

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Faiza Ali
utterances.text: Councilor, thank you for that question.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Faiza Ali
utterances.text: And I think that there are really two parts to that.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Faiza Ali
utterances.text: One is when those incidents occur, it is really important that those are flagged to anyone on the IRC.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Faiza Ali
utterances.text: It could be MOIA.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Faiza Ali
utterances.text: So we are aware and there is documentation.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Faiza Ali
utterances.text: And we often hear from elected officials, but I also want to acknowledge the community-based organization and the mutual aid groups, the Ice Watch groups, frankly, who are on the ground, who often will take pictures, send detailed information.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Faiza Ali
utterances.text: That is really important for us to receive so we can document it and then address it accordingly.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Faiza Ali
utterances.text: I'll say also to the point, and I regret that Councilmember Thomas Henry has left, because we understand that the levels of enforcement across the city have increased tremendously.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Faiza Ali
utterances.text: But the epicenter has been Queens, Elmhurst, and Corona.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Faiza Ali
utterances.text: And so we understand that there is ice walking the streets quite regularly around schools and near city-owned property and parking lots.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Faiza Ali
utterances.text: What we do...

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Faiza Ali
utterances.text: Both in the aftermath when something like this occurs, when we are flagged and an incident took place that there was ICE presence, we're working with local community-based organizations to make sure that we are going out into those communities who have been impacted.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Faiza Ali
utterances.text: We are sharing our Know Your Rights information.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Faiza Ali
utterances.text: We are making sure that folks who have questions and need legal assistance understand that there are city resources that are, in fact, available to them.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Faiza Ali
utterances.text: But I would say...

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Faiza Ali
utterances.text: Documenting those instances, sharing it with City Hall is helpful to us, but communicating with our teams to make sure that we are also

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Faiza Ali
utterances.text: on the ground and working with you to educate our community and provide resources is just as critical.

chapters.summary: Lucero says the school incident Krishnan mentioned was on private property and MOIA engaged with the diocese. Krishnan says his team was there and he believes it was school property, and urges proactive strategies to secure city facilities.
chapters.title: Lucero says school incident was private property; Krishnan disputes

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lorena Lucero
utterances.text: And for the particular instance that you mentioned, Council Member, I believe that happened over the weekend.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lorena Lucero
utterances.text: It was not on NICAP's space.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lorena Lucero
utterances.text: It was actually private property.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lorena Lucero
utterances.text: We were engaging with the diocese, given that it was in their space.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lorena Lucero
utterances.text: But that's part of what the commissioner laid out, because we were made aware there was movement on the back end and coordination amongst agencies to make formal and affirmative communication to find out what was happening on the ground, given what we learned.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: Sir, thank you for your time.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: Now, respectfully, I'm not sure it's 100% accurate because my team was out there, too, and we were in touch with the school, and we saw the footage of it, and I do believe it was actually school property.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: I know that there was a church nearby, and that creates its own issues.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: And I'm not, you know, the reason why I raise it is not so much that that was addressed, and, you know, I'm very appreciative to DOE and the chancellor for speaking with me directly about it to address it.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: I mean more to say.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: I can't, none of us can predict the next time a gate is open in a city parking lot where ICE will use it and come right in because there's no one around in that moment.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: And so definitely a commissioner after the fact, we can talk it through, we can do education work.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: But I would just urge, I'm happy to work with you all on this too, we should come up with some preventative proactive strategies to secure our city property and facilities, especially in neighborhoods where this is happening, so that it doesn't happen again.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: So, you know, yes, after the fact we can address it, but I'd love to come up with ways together to proactively address it because it is a use of city property, whether intended to or not.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: It clearly was not intended to here, but it ends up being a use of city property that is impermissible.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: And so I'd love for us to find a way to protect against that from happening in the first place.

chapters.summary: Krishnan raises private lots with public nexuses, such as the Boulevard parking lot where DOC has offices and the Brooklyn Navy Yard. He asks what the city can do where there is a public component to protect sanctuary laws.
chapters.title: Krishnan raises quasi-public parking lots and public nexus

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: The second instance, which is similar, are parking lots.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: So we have in East Elmhurst, it's outside of my district, but close enough, the Boulevard parking lot, which is a private lot, but the DOC has their offices there.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: Or the Brooklyn Navy Yard, where Cryo Precision

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: has a lease and should not have a lease, and Brooklyn Navy Yard is a public benefit corporation.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: So these are quasi-public private entities.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: Sure, there's a private component to it, but there is also a public nexus as well that I think raises real issues about potential violations of sanctuary laws too, or at least

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: opens the door to the city being far more stringent in enforcement where there is a public nexus.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: And so I know we've done a lot of the administration around private parking lots, but I'm curious about these quasi-private public entities or where there's a public nexus, what we can do, because there's a hook there to do more

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: to protect those areas as well, especially when it comes to parking lots.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Faiza Ali
utterances.text: Yeah, Councilmember, I'm glad you referenced the...

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Faiza Ali
utterances.text: The efforts that the administration has put forward in addressing ICE staging operations in private lots.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Faiza Ali
utterances.text: And I would welcome and continue, I would like to continue these conversations on some of the areas that you just touched on.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: I think those two in particular, and again, I do think that there is a hook there, and I would urge you all to think through and happy to think through with you all as well.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: Where there is a public component, I think that there may be a hook there to be more aggressive and make sure our sanctuary laws are being defended in those instances.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: So we'll look forward to the conversation.

chapters.summary: Krishnan asks what conversations or patrol guide updates are happening to ensure everyday street encounters with ICE do not cross into impermissible cooperation. He notes that public safety rationale can fall into cooperation with a rogue agency.
chapters.title: Krishnan asks NYPD about street encounters and patrol guide

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: Chad, a couple more questions if that's okay.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: My next question, Mr.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: Gerber, is with NYPD.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: We've had a conversation before with Councilman De La Rosa about these instances with NYPD on the ground.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: It is a very real issue, too, and we've talked about it in other contexts.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: with street vendors and otherwise where the law may be, you know, say one thing up here, but on the ground in everyday interactions, things can be different.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: And so there are instances that we've seen, you know, around the city in our districts too, where NYPD police officers are

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: having to work alongside in some capacity with ICE agents.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: Now, I know the rationale could be for public safety, you know, order and maintaining order too, but the other side of that coin is it can fast fall into cooperation, especially with a rogue agency like ICE that will exploit those areas

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: and encourage or create situations where they're being escorted out.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: And they know what they're doing when they do that too, obviously.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: I saw the update to the patrol guide this morning in other contexts with body camera footage.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: I'm wondering what conversations are happening in NYPD or even updates to the patrol guide to ensure on these everyday street encounters we're not crossing into impermissible territory, too, when it comes to our sanctuary laws.

chapters.summary: Gerber says there is an infinite variety of factual scenarios and it is almost impossible to game out every configuration. He says getting supervisors and executives on scene quickly is important, and patrol officers should not have to make these decisions alone.
chapters.title: Gerber explains challenges and elevating decisions

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: And I totally appreciate the question.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: I understand the issue.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: It is incredibly challenging precisely because there's such a, again, I think I said this before, an infinite variety of different factual scenarios, right?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: And trying to game out each possible configuration of what's happening and where the ICE officers are standing and where the cops, it's almost impossible to do.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: I think part of it is, again, getting supervisors and executives on scene as soon as humanly possible.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: That is a big part of it, right?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: Who are just, they have the experience, the training, they're talking to legal bureau executives, they're just,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: they're thinking about the issues that you're talking about, both in terms of not violating the law, not violating policy, and the perception piece, which matters.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: No doubt, it matters.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: I want to come back again, though.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: To the point that, you know, the random patrol officer, you know, in a sector car who ends up stumbling into this, essentially stumbling into it, right?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: It could be literally just driving and seeing it and getting out of the car, what's going on, or a 911 call where...

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: You know, they're, they, they,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: They don't know they're walking into an ICE situation.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: It is such a challenge.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: It is so fraught.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: Our cops are put in incredibly unfair position for reasons out of their control.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: So getting executives on scene is incredibly important.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: And also, by the way, exercising the judgment, right?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: The judgment piece of this, because you've got the optics that you're talking about.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: You have the public safety concerns that are quite real.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: How to navigate that in real time is incredibly hard.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: Asking...

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: You know, someone who just got out of the academy a year ago to figure that out is just unfair.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: We can't ask that of sort of patrol officers.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: That has to get elevated real high, real fast at the department so that executives are making these calls about pulling back.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: Putting the cops in a position to prevent harm with the cost that may come from a perception in terms of perception.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: So, you know, I think I think we do have a better system in place now in terms of things going to operations, operations immediately making those notifications, both on the uniform side and the legal side.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: But I will acknowledge it is it is definitely a work in progress.

chapters.summary: Krishnan asks whether NYPD would withdraw from a task force if it discovered the stated criminal purpose was pretextual and the real purpose was immigration enforcement. Gerber says NYPD would pull out immediately and would be legally required to do so.
chapters.title: Krishnan asks if NYPD would withdraw from pretextual task forces

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: And it is, of course, obviously a very, very real concern for everyone, too, just because of how these street encounters play out.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: My final question is just on that point related to NYPD as well is back in January, you know, at our oversight hearing on sanctuary law compliance too,

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: we talked a lot about the task forces that NYPD is a part of that are, you know, I recognize the complexities there because they could be criminal task forces with federal agencies.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: But sometimes they can be pretext for immigration ICE enforcement operations from federal government.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: If the NYPD discovers that a task force that it's a part of is actually the stated reason for the task force is pretextual and the real reason is immigration enforcement, would NYPD commit to withdrawing from that task force?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: So to be clear, if we were on a task force and we discovered that the task force we were on, which we thought was a criminal task force, was actually in fact a task force devoted to immigration enforcement, we would pull out of that task force immediately.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: We would be legally required to do so, and we would do so.

chapters.summary: Gerber says NYPD knows what its task forces are doing and they are criminal task forces. He says federal agents on those task forces may be detailed to immigration operations, but NYPD detectives will never participate or be detailed for that.
chapters.title: Gerber explains task force nuances and detective restrictions

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: I wanted, though, if I may, it's okay just to speak to some of the nuances here.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: We are aware of what the task forces are doing, right?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: We have obviously detectives there, supervisors there.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: That is not what the task forces that we are doing.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: That is not, they're criminal task forces, each one, you know, different agencies, different focus.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: Now, what does happen, I just want to be clear about this.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: There are times, and again, we saw this more last year, but I'm sure it still happens this year.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: where members of those task forces may get detailed to some immigration enforcement operation, right?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: So again, just I'll use DEA as an example.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: It's not particular to DEA, obviously, but we have detectives on the Drug Enforcement Task Force.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: They are doing narcotics cases.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: You could have DEA agents from that task force who are pulled to assist in some immigration enforcement matter.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: That has happened.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: It may happen in the future.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: Our detectives, under no circumstances, will participate in those activities.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: They will never get pulled for that.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: They will never get detailed for that.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: Our detectives know that.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: Their supervisors know that.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: And we've also made that very clear to our law enforcement partners here in New York.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: The heads of these various agencies in New York, the leadership in New York, is very well aware of our limitations, our restrictions, our policies.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: They understand that our detectives cannot be used in that way.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: I will say, I think they very much value the task forces.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: They want us to continue being in those task forces.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: They do not want to do things that would put our participation in those task forces in jeopardy.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: Does that answer your question?

chapters.summary: Krishnan appreciates Gerber's commitment on task forces and says sanctuary violations can happen on the ground even with good intentions. He raises concerns about DOC contracts and calls being recorded and potentially shared with ICE.
chapters.title: Krishnan thanks NYPD and raises DOC contract concerns

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: It does, and I appreciate the commitment on that, too.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: And I just want to end by saying thank you.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: This is what concerns me the most is, you know, the problematic.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: These problematic areas are sanctuary laws, even if we have the best of intentions, but they're happening on the ground in everyday instances or with parking lots that are open.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: I know with DOC, there's an issue with the contracts, the curists that may raise questions about what's being shared, with calls being recorded and shared, potentially with ICE as well.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: These are all things where we can be so vigilant, but on the ground, the reality can outpace our vigilance in terms of what we are doing to enforce our sanctuary laws.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: And I look forward to working with you all to ensure that we are protecting proactively against those instances too.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: Thank you, Chair.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: Sorry I went over my lot.

chapters.summary: Joseph pushes back on the idea that patrol officers cannot be expected to understand ICE situations. She says community rapid response groups do this without training and that officers should meet that level of awareness.
chapters.title: Joseph pushes back on expectations for patrol officers

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: You all did.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: It's okay.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: You know, and quite frankly, I just want to push back a little bit about...

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: You know, not expecting the patrol officers to really understand what's going on.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: I mean, our everyday citizens, our rapid response groups, they are aware of what a nice vehicle looks like, what license plates are, ICE vehicles, what they're wearing, where they frequent.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: They are expected to understand that world.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: They are doing it without any proper training from any organization.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: They're doing it on their own.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: And we...

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: Are asking them, in essence, to fill that void and do that.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: And so...

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: I think we do require our patrol officers to meet that level of understanding and walking into a situation.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: And I would just end by saying, you know, listen, I was never a police officer, but I was a dean of discipline.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: And I was a dean of discipline in a high school.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: And when I walked into that high school, I had to keep my head on a swivel at all times to understand what was going on and pick up on little things that were happening in that.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: And that is, again, at the lowest form of enforcement to keep people safe.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: And so when we talk about keeping people safe,

utterances.speaker: Elsie Encarnación
utterances.text: keeping people safe and what that means, it means that you are expecting your patrol officers to do that.

utterances.speaker: Elsie Encarnación
utterances.text: So just, just, I just wanted to push back on that statement that we cannot expect them to understand that.

chapters.summary: Gerber says patrol officers do incredible work and know immigration-related situations are a red flag. He clarifies that his point was about difficult public safety and optics decisions in real time, not about officers not knowing the rules.
chapters.title: Gerber clarifies patrol officers and difficult decisions

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: I mean, just, just to be clear, I don't want to be misunderstood.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: And our patrol officers do incredible things every day and deal with incredibly fraught situations every day.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: And I think our patrol officers do very much know, very much know.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: And I think we've done, I do think we've done a good job of making this part of the culture of the department of people knowing, hey, hold on, this is immigration related.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: This is a red flag.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: We've got to be, you know, there are laws and rules.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: We've got to be really, really careful here.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: The point I was just making before is a little bit different, which is.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: And this is what we've been talking about today is sometimes you have these situations where it's not the question is not just a question of the law and the policy.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: It's how are we in a in a certain moment thinking about the public safety concerns that are very real.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: Thinking about also some of the optics issues that are very real, sometimes those things can be intention.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: That's not a question of, hey, what's the rule in the patrol guide?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: That's not what I'm imagining, a question of, you know, what does the law say?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: It's actually making, frankly, sometimes very fraught decisions, tough decisions.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: And by the way, you're right.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: Sometimes patrol officers just have to make those decisions in real time.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: I'm just saying I think it was.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: We have a responsibility as a department, as much as possible, to put those decisions on supervisors.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: And that's what we very much try to do.

chapters.summary: Chair Encarnación asks how the Attorney General's new investigatory powers relate to accountability for local law violations. MOIA says it has been in touch with the AG's office and discussed findings from audits published earlier this year.
chapters.title: Chair asks about AG investigatory powers and accountability

utterances.speaker: Elsie Encarnación
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Elsie Encarnación
utterances.text: I know that the AG has a new investigatory powers.

utterances.speaker: Elsie Encarnación
utterances.text: I wanted to ask how they relate to the question of accountability and how you see that relating to it for the local laws violations.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: Through the IRC, we have been in touch with the AG's office and have discussed some of the findings that we've laid out in the findings and audits that we published earlier this year.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: So we're speaking to the AG's office.

chapters.summary: Chair Encarnación asks MOIA to go on record supporting Intro 1078-A, the DOC-related bill. MOIA says it supports the spirit of both 1077-A and 1078-A but is discussing them with the Law Department.
chapters.title: Chair asks MOIA support for 1078A

utterances.speaker: Elsie Encarnación
utterances.text: Okay, I know we've been focused a lot of the conversations because of NYPD being here around 1077A, but for 1078A, which is a DOC-related one,

utterances.speaker: Elsie Encarnación
utterances.text: can we get you on record, Moya, and your support for that bill?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: Yeah, as I mentioned in our testimony, that these bills in both 1077A and 1078A, we are discussing them with the law department, though we do express support for the spirit of both bills.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: Councilor, you know these are going through the legislative process.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: Which I'm very familiar with.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: And so we're going to continue to engage the council in those conversations.

utterances.speaker: Elsie Encarnación
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Elsie Encarnación
utterances.text: I'm going to try to go through that legislative process as quickly as possible on these bills.

utterances.speaker: Elsie Encarnación
utterances.text: So I hope you're doing the same.

utterances.speaker: Elsie Encarnación
utterances.text: You know where to reach me.

chapters.summary: Chair Encarnación describes the case of 19-year-old Venezuelan immigrant Gutierrez Flores, detained after the Bronx DA declined to prosecute and later handed to FBI custody. She asks NYPD to explain why he was held and transferred.
chapters.title: Chair asks about Gutierrez Flores detention and FBI transfer

utterances.speaker: Elsie Encarnación
utterances.text: So I wanted to specifically ask, and this is about a 19-year-old Venezuelan immigrant.

utterances.speaker: Elsie Encarnación
utterances.text: On February 24th of 2025, Mr.

utterances.speaker: Elsie Encarnación
utterances.text: Gutierrez Flores was arrested by officers in the 52nd precinct in the Bronx and taken to a local precinct.

utterances.speaker: Elsie Encarnación
utterances.text: Overnight, according to media reports, the Bronx DA's office had the

utterances.speaker: Elsie Encarnación
utterances.text: declined to prosecute that case.

utterances.speaker: Elsie Encarnación
utterances.text: And while ordinarily a suspect that the DA declined to prosecute is no longer detainable, Mr.

utterances.speaker: Elsie Encarnación
utterances.text: Gutierrez Flores was detained for much of that next day, February 27th, when he was handed over to FBI custody.

utterances.speaker: Elsie Encarnación
utterances.text: And so my question is whether you can explain in detail why the NYPD continued to detain Mr.

utterances.speaker: Elsie Encarnación
utterances.text: Gutierrez even after the DA declined to prosecute when the FBI indicated that they might pursue federal charges against him.

utterances.speaker: Elsie Encarnación
utterances.text: And when and why was he transferred into FBI custody to the extent that you can express today?

chapters.summary: Gerber says DOI examined the case and found NYPD complied with sanctuary law and policy. He explains the FBI was involved in a gun investigation, the state declined, and the FBI took custody; NYPD later updated policy to vet all custody transfers.
chapters.title: Gerber explains DOI found NYPD complied; policy updated

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: Sure, sure.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: So.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: I don't have all the details in front of me, but I am generally familiar with the matter.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: And I should say, I think, as you know, this was one of the instances that DOI looked at in their report.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: So DOI did a deep dive on this, deep examination.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: And I do want to emphasize that while it certainly informed certain recommendations that they had, DOI found following in their investigation that NYPD did comply.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: With sanctuary city law and with our policies in connection with this incident.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: So I want to start with that.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: I think that's important.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: So if I recall correctly, it was a gun arrest.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: I think critically, this was a investigation the FBI was involved in.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: I forget which of the FBI task forces, but they were involved in the case.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: So it was FBI working with NYPD.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: And then what transpired.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: in terms of the case first being pitched to the DA's office, the DA's office declining, and then the FBI taking the individual into custody in the hopes of the person being prosecuted by the feds.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: Is not unheard of.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: Certainly in a joint investigation like that, sometimes even not in a joint investigation, there'll be a question, so you have a gun case, whether someone's gonna get prosecuted in the state or prosecuted federally, that happens.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: There certainly are situations where, for various reasons, the DA's office passes on a case and the feds are willing to do it and take that case on.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: And so the fact that the FBI, involved in a gun arrest, seeing the state decline, then wanted to try to get the person charged.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: Federally in Southern, that's not shocking or, or for thank you, even that, even that surprising.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: And so to the extent, you know, the person, I would want to know how long the person was held for, but assuming, I mean, depending on the timeframe, it totally, frankly, it's fine.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: The person there's, there's been a probable cause arrest.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: Is the DA's office is declining to prosecute.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: Okay, will Southern do it?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: Hey, the FBI is taking this person to,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: to pitch it to Southern.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: Now, what ends up happening, right, is ultimately Southern does not prosecute the case.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: And then the person is handed over to by the FBI to immigration authorities.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: So again, in terms of

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: Did this violate city law?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: Did it violate our policy at the time?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: And that's what DOI found.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: I will say a point that DOI made, sort of looking at this, they said, look, you didn't violate law or policy, but you want to have more vetting.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: Of a situation like this.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: And the point they made, I recommend these they made, we accepted and have adopted and have implemented in our policy.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: They said, you know, you have this whole process for reviewing transfers of custody

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: in connection with detainers, it shouldn't be limited in that way.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: It should cover situations like this.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: And our policy now does cover situations like this.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: So I mentioned this earlier, but one of the changes that we made coming out of the DOI report was that to have sort of a level of scrutiny, not just on detainer requests, but really any situation in which we're being

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: asked to transfer custody.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: And our policy speaks to that.

chapters.summary: Chair Encarnación asks about guns retrieved in the case. Gerber says he does not have the particulars and cannot speak to the probable cause analysis.
chapters.title: Chair asks about guns in case; Gerber lacks details

utterances.speaker: Elsie Encarnación
utterances.text: And I understand that there were guns retrieved in that case that were located inside of

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: I don't know the particulars of the case.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: I think my vague recollection is that maybe there were, I have in my head there were maybe two people arrested, but you know what, I'm just not sure.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: I don't have all the facts in front of me.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: But I really couldn't speak to like the probable cause analysis in that case.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: That I'm not sure about.

utterances.speaker: Elsie Encarnación
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Elsie Encarnación
utterances.text: So I'm not going to go down that line of questioning because I don't want you to answer something you don't have in front of you.

chapters.summary: Chair Encarnación asks MOIA about its outreach in Marble Hill after the shooting and how many staffers are available. Ali describes immediate site visits, canvassing, and rapid response protocols, and lists languages spoken by MOIA staff.
chapters.title: Chair asks MOIA about Marble Hill outreach and staffing

utterances.speaker: Elsie Encarnación
utterances.text: But I do, and for Moya, I know you were present in Marble Hill the next day after the shooting to distribute flyers containing information about the free legal services, the Know Your Rights cards.

utterances.speaker: Elsie Encarnación
utterances.text: Can you share a little bit more about...

utterances.speaker: Elsie Encarnación
utterances.text: How you approach being president in the neighborhood and sharing that information.

utterances.speaker: Elsie Encarnación
utterances.text: And specifically, can you tell me, like, how many staffers are available to you at a moment's notice when something like this happens that you have to, like, go out and really do outreach?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: Yeah, so, Chair, just to reiterate that when we first learned of the ice shooting in Marble Hill, our senior leadership team at MOIA, along with myself, we immediately went to the site

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: to be present in community and to see how we can offer support in different ways.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: In the days that immediately followed, our senior leadership, along with our community engagement team, returned to the neighborhood to canvas local businesses and schools and talk to residents in buildings to ensure that

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: They had access to know your rights information and resources so they can contact our hotline if they needed legal assistance.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: We, in terms of the question directly on our approach, we worked really closely with some of the local elected officials in that neighborhood, community advocates,

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: informing them that we were going to be there and really serving as the on-site collaboration to make sure that we had a coordinator response.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: As you can imagine, there was a ton of support coming from different levels of government, but from community.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: And I think that that neighborhood was flooded for many days.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: So we wanted to make sure that the information we were giving out was coordinated with everyone else on the ground.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: And in terms of staff that is immediately available, I mean, this is an all-hands-on-deck moment.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: You know, MOIA has our own internal rapid response protocols.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: What do we do in incidents like this that require a significant level of coordination?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: We do have staff members on both our community engagement teams, on our constituent services team that speak a variety of languages to make sure that when we're going out into communities, we're prioritizing the languages in these communities as well.

utterances.speaker: Elsie Encarnación
utterances.text: How many languages?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: I can give you the breakdown, Bayan.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: So we have the commissioner just shared on the Moyes community engagement team, which consists of seven staff members.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: They collectively speak 13 languages.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: English, Mandarin, Cantonese, Fijianese, French, Portuguese, Hakka, Hindi, Urdu, Bengali, German, Fulani, and Wolof.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: We also have a constituent service team of five staff members.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: They, in addition to the languages that I mentioned above, they also speak Spanish, Haitian, Creole, Tibetan, and Korean.

chapters.summary: Chair Encarnación asks how MOIA determines which community organizations to partner with. Ali says MOIA works with over 100 organizations, houses of worship, colleges, senior centers, and schools, prioritizing trusted community-based organizations across all boroughs.
chapters.title: Chair asks how MOIA selects partner organizations

utterances.speaker: Elsie Encarnación
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Elsie Encarnación
utterances.text: And when you talk about partnership and organizations that you partner with, does the community engagement team, how do you determine which organizations to partner with?

utterances.speaker: Elsie Encarnación
utterances.text: And what is, like, do you seek out new organizations?

utterances.speaker: Elsie Encarnación
utterances.text: Do you rely on organizations coming to you?

utterances.speaker: Elsie Encarnación
utterances.text: I mean, there's so many.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: I'll start, and I'm sure Lenna will piggyback and see if there are any details that I leave out.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: I mean, we work really closely with over 100 organizations based in communities, both our contractor providers and other organizations

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: like the New York Immigration Coalition, like Hands Off NYC, the Chinese American Planning Council, Make the Road, NILAC, Live On, and many others.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: We also partner with houses of worship and faith leaders.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: You know, we work with colleges and senior centers and community centers along with our public schools to make sure that we're reaching immigrant New Yorkers where they live, where they work, and where they gather.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: In terms of how we identify those partners, some of that is natural work that we're doing, you know, with our programs.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: We want to make sure that we're covering all five boroughs.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: I know Councilmember Hanks was here earlier, and I was so excited to share with her some of the organizations we work with on the ground in the Great Borough of Staten Island.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: We want to make sure that we have partnerships in communities that have large and dense immigrant neighborhoods.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: that these organizations maybe speak particular languages that we need in order to educate the community about their rights and organizations.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: Of course, we prioritize community-based organizations, ones that have trust in communities that we can partner with and make sure that we have strong, you know, that also have strong relationships with the local residents.

chapters.summary: Chair Encarnación asks about the timeline for Local Law 114 signage. MOIA says the overwhelming majority of covered agencies have posted required signage, with 37 of 42 agencies compliant, and a report is due November 30.
chapters.title: Chair asks about Local Law 114 signage timeline

utterances.speaker: Elsie Encarnación
utterances.text: I know and I believe in your opening testimony, you mentioned that the signage on the local law 114 was in progress.

utterances.speaker: Elsie Encarnación
utterances.text: Is there a timeline as to where in the timeline we are?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: As of this morning, the overwhelming majority of covered agencies have, in fact, posted the required signage, and we're looking forward to working towards full compliance.

utterances.speaker: Elsie Encarnación
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Elsie Encarnación
utterances.text: Bye.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: Well, as of today, we have 37 out of the 42 agencies that have posted the required signage in their buildings, and we are prepared.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: I know that we have a report that is due to the council at the end of this month on November 30th, and we are fully prepared to provide updates at that time.

utterances.speaker: Elsie Encarnación
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Elsie Encarnación
utterances.text: I'm going to take a pause now so that Councilmember Aviles could do her round two.

chapters.summary: Avilés notes that many federal agencies have been deputized to do civil immigration enforcement. She asks how many task forces exist and what safeguards prevent agents with dual roles from using NYPD resources for immigration enforcement.
chapters.title: Avilés asks about task forces and deputized federal agents

utterances.speaker: Alexa Avilés
utterances.text: Thank you, Chair.

utterances.speaker: Alexa Avilés
utterances.text: I just wanted to follow up on a couple of things, particularly with the task force issue.

utterances.speaker: Alexa Avilés
utterances.text: I guess I wanted to first note, well, I assume you are aware that the United States Marshal Service, DEA, ATF,

utterances.speaker: Alexa Avilés
utterances.text: BOP, IRS, Department of State, UCIS, among others, have all been deputized to do civil immigration enforcement.

utterances.speaker: Alexa Avilés
utterances.text: Now, you know where I'm going.

utterances.speaker: Alexa Avilés
utterances.text: We understand that there are quite a number of task forces, so I'd love for you to clarify for the record how many task forces are in existence and really walk me through in very clear detail

utterances.speaker: Alexa Avilés
utterances.text: how is it, what safeguards are in place for

utterances.speaker: Alexa Avilés
utterances.text: agents that have multiple roles, whether the task force is set for criminal investigations, however, those same agents are also doing civil immigration enforcement and have been deputized to do so.

utterances.speaker: Alexa Avilés
utterances.text: How does NYPD safeguard

utterances.speaker: Alexa Avilés
utterances.text: not breaking the law and using our city resources.

utterances.speaker: Alexa Avilés
utterances.text: So you know what I'm asking.

chapters.summary: Gerber says there are roughly 20 to 25 task forces and acknowledges federal agents on them may be pulled for immigration enforcement. He says NYPD detectives are never part of that and would face charges and specs if they were.
chapters.title: Gerber says 20-25 task forces; detectives not pulled for immigration

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: Yeah, sure, sure.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: A few things.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: So in terms of the number of task forces, there's somewhere between 20 and 25 task forces total.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: I don't have the full list in front of me, but it's going to be roughly in the 20 to 25 range.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: And, you know, I don't know the exact list, but yes, what happened last year was all these federal agencies that previously did not have Title VIII authority all of a sudden got Title VIII authority and were pulled.

utterances.speaker: Alexa Avilés
utterances.text: And we see them engage in civil immigration.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: Yes, yes, 100%.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: Again, I think certainly we saw a lot of this in early, in the mid-2025.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: I do think my sense of it, sense of it is that New York City, there is less of this.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: now, but it certainly is a phenomenon.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: No question.

utterances.speaker: Alexa Avilés
utterances.text: I would suggest you're not making that assumption that it's less.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: So what ends up happening, right, is, sure, our detectives are on a task force, and there are members of that task force who then get pulled.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: Like for details, for civil immigration enforcement, for immigration enforcement details.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: Our detectives are never part of that, ever.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: If they were to be a part of that, I'd be very blunt.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: If our detectives were to get pulled with special agents to do some immigration enforcement, I mean,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: I mean, they would face charges and specs.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: They'd be pulled from the task force.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: Frankly, I would expect us to pull out of that task force.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: Right?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: In other words,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: To the extent there are agents on those task forces who then go, not involving our detectives at all, on a pull for civil immigration enforcement, yes, that has happened, that happens.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: But our detectives are not part of that.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: These task forces,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: We know what they're doing.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: They're doing criminal cases, very significant criminal cases, important for the safety and security of the city and New Yorkers.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: And our detectives are part of that.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: And I will add that doing the audit and doing the audit, we're going to do it going forward annually, is part of this effort, right?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: It's the check.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: Hey, are we seeing things where it looks like maybe there is somehow, some way, some blurring?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: And like I said, anyone who's doing that, and the cops know this, detectives know this, the consequences of crossing that line are severe.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: Severe for individual...

chapters.summary: Avilés says task forces intermingle and build relationships, making lines blurry. She asks how NYPD ensures information is not shared with ICE through task forces, databases, license plate readers, or technology vendors.
chapters.title: Avilés questions task force blurring and information sharing

utterances.speaker: Alexa Avilés
utterances.text: Specifically for the task forces, you're saying?

utterances.speaker: Alexa Avilés
utterances.text: Well, I'm saying I think that...

utterances.speaker: Alexa Avilés
utterances.text: Because, I mean, we've seen a good number of evidence over the years where the lines have been blurred and, you know, people have not obeyed by those lines.

utterances.speaker: Alexa Avilés
utterances.text: I think what we need to understand is while you can provide a directive...

utterances.speaker: Alexa Avilés
utterances.text: There are still these task force that are intermingled, that are building relationships.

utterances.speaker: Alexa Avilés
utterances.text: that are having informal conversations, and yet we are expected that everyone understands the lines.

utterances.speaker: Alexa Avilés
utterances.text: I'm not so sure I trust that, but how do we ensure our residents that these task forces are not places

utterances.speaker: Alexa Avilés
utterances.text: where the lines are blurred and information is shared.

utterances.speaker: Alexa Avilés
utterances.text: And I think I'd love also for you to talk about specifically what kind of information NYPD shares with ICHSI or any other federal agencies through its databases.

utterances.speaker: Alexa Avilés
utterances.text: Through its real-time crime center, through license plate readers, technology vendors, or any other information sharing arrangements.

chapters.summary: Gerber says consequences for misconduct are severe and federal partners know NYPD may pull out of task forces. He says no federal agency has direct access to NYPD systems, but information is shared in joint criminal investigations.
chapters.title: Gerber explains incentives and no direct federal access to NYPD systems

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: So the first part of that, I think the key, right, is to create

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: not just have the right rules in place, to your point, but also to have the appropriate incentive structure, right?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: So for the detectives to know that if they are doing things they're not supposed to be doing, the consequences for them and their careers will be severe.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: It's also being very clear with the task forces from the federal side.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: They know.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
